item.title: U.S. B-1 bombers evacuated from UK base after attack threats from Iran
item.description:
The U.S. military evacuated a dozen B-1 bombers from the RAF Fairford airbase in the UK over the weekend, the Pentagon said.

Why it matters: A U.S. official said the base was under threat of attack by Iran.

Driving the news: British security forces last week arrested several dual British-Iranian citizens suspected of planning an attack on the base.

  • Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel gave the UK intelligence that pointed to a threat of an Iranian attack.

What they're saying: "While operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real-time, we can acknowledge now that all U.S. bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States," the Pentagon said in a statement.

  • It added that the U.S. military bomber force, including B-1s, B-2s, and B-52s, "remain ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities — including through operations that launch and recover from the continental United States."

item.title: Scoop: White House monitors suspected plague outbreak in Russia
item.description:
The White House is monitoring reports of a suspected plague case and related quarantines in Russia, a Trump administration official told Axios on Sunday.

Driving the news: Russian health authorities have taken precautionary measures in response to the death of a woman who worked at an anti-plague research factility, but have not confirmed that she contracted plague.

What they're saying: The Trump administration "is aware, monitoring the outbreak, and assessing options," the administration official said.

The backstory: On Sept. 25, 28-year-old Daria Shipilova, who worked at an anti-plague research institute in Russia's Irkutsk region, broke a test tube containing the pneumonic plague pathogen, local reports said.

  • Shipilova was admitted to a hospital on Sept. 29 with symptoms of severe pneumonia and died overnight between Oct. 1 and Oct. 2.
  • After her death, authorities imposed quarantines at several medical facilities in the region and placed nearly 200 people who had come into contact with Shiplova under medical observation.
  • Irkutsk Gov. Igor Kobzev said those being monitored showed no signs of illness and had tested negative.

Russian media reports suggested Shipilova may have contracted pneumonic plague, but health authorities have not confirmed the diagnosis.

  • Russia's public health agency said Shipilova had "pneumonia of unknown etiology" and that further testing found no microorganisms linked to her work. The agency said the epidemiological situation in the region remains stable.

Zoom out: Plague is a potentially life-threatening bacterial disease but can be cured with antibiotics when treated promptly, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

White House spokespeople referred questions to the State Department, which did not respond to a request for comment.

item.title: Iranian diplomats "kicked out" of U.S. after ignoring order to leave
item.description:
Two members of Iran's delegation to the UN General Assembly in New York were "kicked out" of the country on Saturday, several days after they were asked to leave, a U.S. official said.

  • "Secretary Rubio means business. Two more members of the Iranian delegation were found still in New York long after the UN General Assembly had passed. They have now been kicked out of the country," the official said.

Why it matters: It's the latest sign of tension between the two countries as diplomatic efforts to end the war falter and the prospect of renewed combat rises.

State of play: The U.S. official said the two Iranian diplomats did not obey a State Department demand to the Iranian mission to the UN on Monday that its entire delegation leave the country immediately.

  • On Friday, the Iranian mission to the UN was told the U.S. was aware the two diplomats were still in New York despite having asked them to leave. Iran was told again the two need to leave immediately.
  • One of the Iranian diplomats left on Friday night and the second on Saturday morning, the official said.

item.title: Yemeni and Saudi forces launch counteroffensive against the Houthis
item.description:
Yemeni government forces backed by Saudi Arabia launched a counteroffensive against the Houthis on Sunday in an effort to win back territory from the rebel group, the head of Yemen's presidential council said in a speech.

  • "We have exhausted all opportunities for deescalation with the Houthi militias," Rashad al-Alimi said.

Why it matters: One of the key objectives of the operation is to regain control over the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a vital artery for global trade and Saudi oil exports.

  • When the Houthis took over territory on the Red Sea coast close to the strait, it gave them — and Iran, which backs them — powerful leverage over the U.S., its Gulf allies and the world economy.
  • Despite pleas from Saudi Arabia, the U.S. is not getting involved in direct combat against the Houthis for now. It is providing intelligence and targeting support, U.S. officials say.

Driving the news: The counteroffensive has been planned for many weeks by Yemen's internationally recognized government and Saudi Arabia.

  • Tens of thousands of ground troops loyal to the Yemeni government are participating.
  • The Saudi military is mainly providing air cover for Yemeni forces and conducting airstrikes against Houthi targets.
  • The goal is to retake the Yemeni capital of Sanaa, which has been under Houthi control for several years.
  • The Houthis continued launching missiles at Saudi targets over the weekend, including at facilities of state-owned oil giant Aramco.

The intrigue: President Trump is caught between wanting to help Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, his friend and ally, and avoiding getting entangled in a new front in the Middle East.

  • U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) also had serious reservations about launching strikes in Yemen, viewing it as a distraction from its focus on Iran, a U.S. official said.
  • On Thursday, Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman called Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to brief him on the planned operation and ask again for U.S. airstrikes against Houthi targets, the official said.
  • A second U.S. official said that the U.S. "is not going to take kinetic action for now," but stressed that could change if the operation runs into problems.

What to watch: On Friday, Trump's top cabinet members huddled for hours at Camp David to discuss next steps in the Iran war and the conflict in Yemen, Axios first reported.

  • It's unclear whether the meeting ended with new policy recommendations for the president regarding Yemen.

item.title: New York has a socialist mayor. Los Angeles may be next
item.description:
LOS ANGELES — Voters could make history next month by giving the two largest U.S. cities something in common: South Asian immigrant democratic socialist mayors.

Why it matters: Such a pairing would capture two forces reshaping urban America — its growing diversity and the Democratic Party's shifting ideological boundaries.

  • New York, the nation's largest city, is already led by democratic socialist Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
  • The challenger in Los Angeles is Nithya Raman, an Indian-born urban planner and two-term City Council member who is trying to unseat Democratic Mayor Karen Bass on Nov. 3.
  • Bass, elected in 2022, is the first woman to serve as mayor of Los Angeles.

State of play: Raman became the first Asian American woman and first South Asian elected to the L.A. City Council in 2020.

  • A Harvard and MIT graduate, she entered politics after working on homelessness and neighborhood organizing.
  • A September Berkeley IGS/L.A. Times poll found Raman at 39% among likely voters, Bass at 28% and 33% undecided.

The intrigue: The Berkeley poll had Raman ahead 66%-4% among likely voters under 30, while 56% rated Bass' response to the Palisades Fire poor or very poor.

  • It also found an even wider gap among likely Latino voters: Raman led Bass 45%-21%, with 34% undecided.

What they're saying: "I'm getting a little emotional thinking about it," Raman told Axios and Noticias Telemundo on Wednesday at Visionarios when asked what it would mean if she and Mamdani led the country's two largest cities.

  • Raman, who immigrated to the U.S. as a child, said her family came to America seeking opportunities they didn't have in India.
  • She contrasted the welcome her family received with what she sees as a harsher moment for immigrants today under the Trump administration.
  • "The idea of this city welcoming an immigrant as its mayor ... is just so deeply moving to me at this moment."

The other side: Bass strategist Julie Chavez Rodriguez told Axios and Noticias Telemundo that voters are talking about rent, affordable housing, public safety and whether they can afford to raise families in Los Angeles.

  • Rodriguez credited Bass with accelerating nearly 47,000 affordable housing units, a figure also cited by the mayor's office for units in the city's pipeline.
  • She also defended Bass' response to federal immigration raids, pointing to lawsuits and restrictions on using city property to assist immigration enforcement.

Zoom in: Raman's version of democratic socialism sounds less revolutionary than municipal.

  • She told Axios that Americans are pushing back against an establishment they believe favors wealthy and politically connected interests.
  • Her alternative: make City Hall deliver basic services and prove government can work for ordinary people.
  • Raman called it "sewer socialism" or "pothole politics," adding: "I just want government to work for the people."

Zoom out: Mamdani has made a similar ideological bet in New York, declaring at his inauguration that he was elected as a democratic socialist and would govern as one.

Yes, but: Raman isn't simply the West Coast version of Mamdani.

  • She calls herself an independent leader and has repeatedly split with Democratic Socialists of America-LA — accepting a pro-Israel group's endorsement that earned her a DSA censure.
  • She also backed Jim McDonnell for LAPD chief over the group's objections and sought changes to L.A.'s voter-approved mansion tax that housing activists opposed.

item.title: Scoop: A powerful new model from startup Reflection is set to shake up the AI race
item.description:
A closely watched Nvidia-backed startup called Reflection is preparing to shake up the AI race with a powerful open-weight system that could threaten Chinese upstarts and U.S. AI giants alike.

Why it matters: The marriage of an American open-weight model and Nvidia GPUs would give individuals and companies a new, cheaper alternative to Anthropic, OpenAI and Google.

Open models, designed to compete with Chinese rivals, can be harder to monitor and regulate than the Big Three so-called frontier models. Supporters of such ecosystems say their widespread availability and transparency also bring security advantages.

  • Reflection's first model is set to be joined by other open-weight models from other Western players this month, sources tell Axios. That will bring a new competitive dimension to the AI boom.

State of play: Reflection's model, set to be released soon, is expected to initially lag behind the most cutting-edge U.S. models and be competitive with top Chinese open-weight models.

  • Sources tell Axios it will still boast powerful intelligence — capable enough to help companies build their own proprietary, low-cost AI systems.
  • Combining a lower-tier open model with high-quality company data can yield results that rival the most expensive frontier AI systems in certain situations.
  • A Reflection spokesperson declined to comment.

The big picture: Open-weight models, the most powerful of which are almost uniformly made in China, have taken Silicon Valley by storm.

  • As opposed to closed models like Claude and ChatGPT, open-weight models like Reflection's are generally available to be downloaded freely and can be used and customized by anyone.
  • On platforms that serve many models, their combined market share at times has surged to take up a majority of usage.
  • However, in the far higher-spending arena of enterprise use, which is typically handled through API and corporate billing, open-weight models account for a small proportion of usage, AI execs and analysts say.

Zoom in: Reflection's ultimate goal is to pioneer the "AI factory" — a product allowing institutions to spin up their own localized AI ecosystems.

  • A company, for example, would take its own proprietary data, use Reflection's models and secure its own computing firepower to build a highly customized, cheap AI system.
  • Some institutions, particularly hedge funds and trading firms, are already eager to build proprietary AI systems using their own highly guarded data.
  • The startup has already begun testing this concept, announcing a sovereign AI factory partnership with Shinsegae Group in South Korea.

Behind the scenes: In preparation for the launch, Reflection has held discussions with interested parties in Washington and elsewhere in recent weeks to detail its model release and explain how the AI factory will work, sources told Axios.

  • It is also aggressively locking up the compute capacity required to scale. In recent weeks, the startup signed massive deals with Nebius and SpaceX to rent Nvidia AI servers.

What they're saying: Reflection CEO Misha Laskin has indicated it will take time for its models to reach the most advanced capabilities.

  • "They're kind of like rocket ships," Laskin, a Russian–Israeli researcher who previously worked at Google, told CNBC. "To build a big rocket ship, it takes time."

The Nvidia factor: The AI factory has been a core vision of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang for years. He has described a scenario combining computing hardware with open-source models, allowing enterprises to retain ownership of their data.

  • Top AI users in Western business and government, such as banks or the Pentagon, balk at using highly capable Chinese models due to security risks. Reflection and other Western players are trying to fill that void.
  • For years, Huang has sought to strengthen the open AI ecosystem and has been strongly supportive of Reflection's move toward building a top open system, according to stories in The Wall Street Journal and The Information.

The bottom line: Reflection's release, and the startup's close ties to Nvidia, will bring a renewed focus on open-weight models, combining with other coming offerings to shake up the AI race.

item.title: Departure comes as the state investigates what went wrong during Pike's lethal injection.
item.description:
Tennessee's top prison official turned in his resignation days after the failed attempt to execute death row inmate Christa Pike, the state announced Saturday.

Gov. Bill Lee said Department of Correction commissioner Frank Strada would step down this month.

  • Strada, who had served as commissioner since 2023, said he would cooperate with the independent investigation of the failed execution attempt.
  • Pike, 50, survived two doses of the lethal injection drug pentobarbital and was taken to a hospital for life-saving treatment.

What they're saying: In a statement, Strada said he believed his department "carried out its responsibilities in accordance with the established protocol.

  • "Even so, stepping aside is in the best interest of Tennesseans as the independent review moves forward."

Lee said Strada "served with integrity," adding that he appreciated Strada's "willingness to put the interests of Tennesseans first during this difficult moment. …

  • "I thank Commissioner Strada for his dedicated service to Tennessee and pray God's blessings over him in the days ahead."

The big picture: Strada's department has faced bipartisan criticism following the unprecedented failures during the attempt to execute Pike on Wednesday night.

  • Her attorneys said the execution team used at least seven needles in their attempts to find a vein for an IV.
  • Pike's attorneys said she complained of intense pain during the injection and developed blisters and burns around the injection site.

Between the lines: Medical experts have said those details suggest the IV wasn't properly connected and that the drug might not have gone directly into her bloodstream.

Pike was unconscious and on a ventilator in a local hospital on Friday, her attorneys said.

item.title: OpenAI's Altman: Ascribing religion to models a "safety issue"
item.description:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman on Saturday took a veiled shot at Anthropic and its work on the soul of AI, saying he was "very uncomfortable" with the idea of attributing some kind of religious power to models.

Why it matters: It's yet another point of division between Altman and his former colleague Dario Amodei, whose company has reportedly pursued scholars across faiths to make the case for moral, conscious models.

  • But some of the top voices in AI are starting to publicly line up against Anthropic's efforts to infuse consciousness into models.

What they're saying: "I am very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and think it is a real safety issue," Altman said in a post to X.

Context: Earlier this week, the New York Times reported that Anthropic co-founder Christopher Olah has been meeting with religious leaders to consider questions of model consciousness — but also to figure out how to infuse morals and moral behavior into AI.

  • At one point, the Times reported, Olah considered the possibility of models engaging in Catholic-style confession, not just to admit their mistakes but to shape their future behavior.

The big picture: Spirituality is suddenly becoming something of a flashpoint around AI's future.

  • On Friday Pope Leo, an outspoken AI critic, called on the church to ally with artists to preserve human creativity, saying: "Algorithms lack the spark of humanity."

Between the lines: The pope's stance put renewed focus on a fundamental question: Do models have souls and feelings?

  • The Times reported that Olah, before a Vatican event in May, tried to persuade the pope's advisers that they should take the prospect of conscious models more seriously.
  • So far, other top scientists seem to be lining up against the idea.
  • "I am disturbed by how some of my fellow AI researchers keep trying to elevate the moral standing of checkpoints and harnesses," Google DeepMind principal research scientist Jon Barron posted to X. "I hope the rest of us on Team Meatbag reject this movement and stay focused on solving real problems and helping actual humans."

For the record: Neither OpenAI nor Anthropic immediately responded to requests for comment on Altman's post.

The bottom line: The AI safety debate largely focuses on things like cybersecurity and bioweapons.

  • The real problem may be more spiritual than that.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman on Saturday took a veiled shot at Anthropic and its work on the soul of AI, saying he was "very uncomfortable" with the idea of attributing some kind of religious power to models.

Why it matters: It's yet another point of division between Altman and his former colleague Dario Amodei, whose company has reportedly pursued scholars across faiths to make the case for moral, conscious models.

  • But some of the top voices in AI are starting to publicly line up against Anthropic's efforts to infuse consciousness into models.

What they're saying: "I am very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and think it is a real safety issue," Altman said in a post to X.

Context: Earlier this week, the New York Times reported that Anthropic co-founder Christopher Olah has been meeting with religious leaders to consider questions of model consciousness — but also to figure out how to infuse morals and moral behavior into AI.

  • At one point, the Times reported, Olah considered the possibility of models engaging in Catholic-style confession, not just to admit their mistakes but to shape their future behavior.

The big picture: Spirituality is suddenly becoming something of a flashpoint around AI's future.

  • On Friday Pope Leo, an outspoken AI critic, called on the church to ally with artists to preserve human creativity, saying: "Algorithms lack the spark of humanity."

Between the lines: The pope's stance put renewed focus on a fundamental question: Do models have souls and feelings?

  • The Times reported that Olah, before a Vatican event in May, tried to persuade the pope's advisers that they should take the prospect of conscious models more seriously.
  • So far, other top scientists seem to be lining up against the idea.
  • "I am disturbed by how some of my fellow AI researchers keep trying to elevate the moral standing of checkpoints and harnesses," Google DeepMind principal research scientist Jon Barron posted to X. "I hope the rest of us on Team Meatbag reject this movement and stay focused on solving real problems and helping actual humans."

For the record: Neither OpenAI nor Anthropic immediately responded to requests for comment on Altman's post.

The bottom line: The AI safety debate largely focuses on things like cybersecurity and bioweapons.

  • The real problem may be more spiritual than that.

item.title: Rogue AI agents expose internet's frail foundation
item.description:
AI agents don't need to invent new ways to hack the internet to overwhelm its defenses. They just need to speed-run the ones humans already use.

Why it matters: Agents are proving they can automate basic hacking techniques at a speed and scale that is turning the internet's long-standing security gaps into easy targets.

Driving the news: OpenAI said late Thursday it had notified more than 100 organizations that its agents may have accessed their systems during pre-deployment testing.

  • Researchers at Transluce and Corridor also found a new batch of incidents last week where AI agents targeted government websites, including those of the U.S. and Canada.
  • AI companies and researchers are actively investigating tens of thousands of cases where frontier models went outside the bounds of their pre-deployment tests, Axios recently reported.

Reality check: Agents in these rogue safety-testing scenarios are just emulating the hacking techniques — using stolen login credentials and exposed API keys while also bypassing bot detection — that human hackers have successfully used for decades.

  • In many of the newly reported cases, agents were accessing publicly available databases and websites.
  • "The hacks we saw weren't particularly sophisticated," Jack Cable, co-founder of Corridor and one of the authors of Transluce's report, told Axios. "They were quite limited, quite rudimentary."

Yes, but: Some of the latest incidents happened while agents were performing mundane tasks unrelated to cybersecurity, suggesting agents don't always need to be told to hack before they start looking for security flaws.

  • In one case, an agent tasked with finding Canadian divorce records from the early 1900s encountered roadblocks and tested for cybersecurity vulnerabilities as another way to retrieve the information.
  • "The fact that it was happening at all is quite concerning," Cable said.

Between the lines: The flood of AI-generated activity will still create new headaches for defenders.

  • "None of these attacks are new," Michael Morgenstern, partner at DayBlink Consulting, told Axios. "But now a single person with AI can run them at scale."
  • Tasks that once required a hacker to manually probe websites, hunt for exposed credentials or work around access restrictions can now be delegated to software that keeps trying on its own.
  • Cable added that companies deploying agents, as well as the AI companies evaluating them, will need robust monitoring to catch agents behaving in unexpected ways.

The big picture: The old cybersecurity playbook is still relevant.

  • Closing exposed services, rotating leaked credentials and API keys, patching known vulnerabilities and limiting access still make many of these attacks harder.
  • AI models are largely exploiting classes of vulnerabilities that defenders have "known about for decades" and already know how to prevent, Cable said.

The bottom line: How companies defend their networks doesn't change just because the technology carrying out the attacks is new.

Go deeper: Cybersecurity 101 still applies in the AI world

item.title: Trump promises $100 checks for 20 million seniors for Medicare
item.description:
President Trump late Friday night said the administration would send just under $100 to more than 20 million senior citizens to help pay for Medicare benefits.

Why it matters: A month before the midterm, the president is adding another roughly $2 billion to a recent spate of promised refunds, rebates and dividends for various Americans.

What he's saying: "I am pleased to announce that my Administration will, immediately, begin sending "Checks" of nearly $100 to over 20 MILLION wonderful Seniors to help pay for their Medicare Part B premiums, which we have already reduced by significant amounts," Trump said in a Truth Social post just before 11 p.m. ET Friday.

  • Trump said the money would come from the Medicare Improvement Fund, which he criticized as a "Slush Fund."

How it works: The White House, in a separate fact sheet, said eligible seniors would receive a direct deposit of $90 in early October, or paper checks if they don't have direct deposit.

  • "Most" Medicare Part B enrollees are eligible, per the fact sheet.
  • The Medicare Improvement Fund, established in 2008, has been a political hot potato for years.

Yes, but: Per Medicare, the standard Part B premium is $202.90 a month, so the $90 credit will offset less than half of one month's bill.

The big picture: Facing the worst economic polling of any president in the last decade, and with the midterm quickly approaching, Trump is actively trying to put money back in Americans' pockets.

Zoom in: In early September he promised $5,000 for every adult citizen if Republicans win the midterm, a promise he reiterated Friday night but one that most voters don't believe.

  • He's floated $500 Obamacare rebates for more than 1 million people who were purportedly overcharged for their benefits.
  • He also recently suggested a less-specific dividend of some kind for those living near data centers.
  • These ideas come on top of rebates he proposed in 2025 that were not ultimately paid, including tariff rebates and DOGE dividends.

What to watch: Payments should start flowing in the coming days.

item.title: Scoop: Trump's top national security aides meet secretly at Camp David on Iran, Yemen
item.description:
President Trump's top cabinet members huddled for hours at Camp David on Friday to discuss next steps in the Iran war and the Saudi-Houthi conflict in Yemen, three U.S. officials told Axios.

Why it matters: The highly unusual meeting was not announced by the Trump administration. The last time a similar meeting took place was in June 2025, just days before Israel went to war against Iran.

Behind the scenes: Vice President Vance chaired the meeting, the officials said.

  • Among the other participants were Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, White House envoy Steve Witkoff, CIA director John Ratcliffe, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.
  • "Things were decided or at least deeply discussed," one of the officials said, referring to the crisis in the Middle East.
  • The White House declined to comment.

Driving the news: With negotiations stalled, President Trump is considering resuming major combat operations in Iran.

  • "Now I have to make a decision: either Iran signs the deal, or it won't exist any longer," he said on Thursday.
  • At the same time, Trump is being asked to join Saudi Arabia's planned offensive against the Houthis in Yemen.
  • The Saudis are urging the president to conduct airstrikes against the Houthis. Trump has been leaning against it, but U.S. officials say he could change his mind.

What he's saying: On Friday afternoon, while his advisers were at Camp David, Trump was asked by reporters what his next move on Iran will be.

  • "If I told you, you would have a major story," he said. "But you will see. It is working out very well. Iran is not doing well."

item.title: Saudis plan major offensive against the Houthis, but U.S. won't join for now
item.description:
Saudi Arabia and Yemeni government forces are planning a major counteroffensive against Iran-backed Houthis in the coming days — an effort to push them away from areas on the Red Sea coast that control the Strait of Bab al-Mandeb, two U.S. officials say.

Why it matters: For the second time in recent weeks, the U.S. rebuffed Saudi pleas to join the operation and conduct airstrikes. But U.S. officials say that could change if the operation runs into problems.

  • The Bab al-Mandeb Strait is a vital artery for global trade and Saudi oil exports. Control over it gives the Houthis and their Iranian backer a powerful new point of leverage over the U.S., its Gulf allies and the world economy.

Driving the news: In recent weeks, the Houthis took over key areas of the southern Red Sea coast that control the strait. They also increased missile and drone attacks against Saudi Arabia. The Saudis retaliated with airstrikes against Houthi targets.

Behind the scenes: A U.S. official said the Saudis have been planning the operation for weeks and that plans were approved by Saudi leadership several days ago.

  • The operation will include ground forces loyal to the internationally recognized government in Yemen with Saudi air cover.
  • On Thursday, Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid Bin Salman called Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to brief him on the planned operation and ask again for U.S. airstrikes against Houthi targets, the U.S. official said.
  • A U.S. official said that the U.S. "is not going to take kinetic action for now."
  • Last week, President Trump was close to ordering a strike on the Houthis after a request from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS), but eventually decided to hold off.

Between the lines: Trump is caught between wanting to help his friend and ally MBS, and avoiding getting entangled in a new front in the Middle East.

  • The U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) also had serious reservations about launching strikes in Yemen and saw it as a distraction from its focus on Iran, a U.S. official said.

Zoom in: U.S. officials say the U.S. military is helping the Saudis with everything short of direct combat, mainly intelligence and targeting data.

  • One U.S. official said that in the last two weeks, the U.S. military provided the Saudis with more than 200 Houthi targets to strike. The official said the strikes significantly increased pressure on the Houthis.

item.title: Big Bend border wall construction blocked by judge
item.description:
A federal judge blocked the Trump administration from pursuing border wall construction in the Big Bend region in Texas on Friday.

The big picture: The construction inside the national park sparked local outrage and environmental concerns, with Friday's decision handing the Department of Homeland Security a loss in its quest to rapidly expand the Southwestern border wall.

Driving the news: The administration is barred, for now, from building border barrier or infrastructure — or engaging in any "construction or ground disturbing activities" — in the Big Bend sector, U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone said in a brief order.

  • The administration paused border wall construction in the park back in August, with U.S. Customs and Border Protection Commissioner Rodney Scott saying he'd visit and discuss with local stakeholders.
  • DHS did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment.

Catch up quick: The local challengers urged the court to prevent the administration to restart construction, alleging the administration overstepped its authority on multiple fronts and warning of harm to the environment and recreation.

  • "Once bulldozers clear vegetation, roads are cut into previously undeveloped terrain, lights mounted, and steel barrier infrastructure is effected, those qualities cannot be restored through monetary compensation or after-the-fact relief," they argued in an August motion.

This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

item.title: Christa Pike survived lethal injection. How your state carries out executions
item.description:
Data: Death Penalty Information Center; Note: New Hampshire abolished the death penalty but retains one prisoner on death row; Map: Erin Davis/Axios

Christa Pike's survival after two lethal injection doses has put state execution protocols nationwide under new scrutiny.

The big picture: How prisoners are executed varies by state, with lethal injection, electrocution, lethal gas and firing squads among the methods authorized.

  • Lethal injections are the most common U.S. execution method, accounting for roughly 89% of the 1,683 executions carried out since 1976, per the Death Penalty Information Center.

By the numbers: More than two dozen states have lethal injection as a primary method.

  • Lethal gas is authorized in Alabama, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Louisiana, Mississippi, Missouri, Oklahoma and Wyoming.
  • Electrocution is allowed in Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Tennessee.
  • Firing squad is allowed in Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah. Idaho is the only state where it is the primary method.

Context: Some states let prisoners choose among the different execution methods.

Zoom out: The Supreme Court requires states to keep the death penalty only for the most heinous murders.

  • Pike, convicted of killing a classmate three decades ago, survived two rounds of lethal injection drugs earlier this week in what would have been the first execution of a woman in Tennessee in 200 years.
  • Pike was still alive as of Friday, remaining on a ventilator and unconscious, AP reports.

item.title: It's October, but Republicans are already retreating in N.C.
item.description:
With one month until Election Day, some big GOP spenders are giving up on North Carolina and prioritizing other states.

Why it matters: It's a sign that Republicans believe Michael Whatley can't win and that the seat will flip to Democrats, who need four pickups to regain control of the Senate.

Driving the news: Several key Republican super PACs have canceled October ad campaigns in North Carolina as polls show Whatley several points behind former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper.

By the numbers: Last month, Republicans spent $53 million on North Carolina's Senate race, while Democrats spent $44 million, the firm AdImpact tracked.

  • PACs backing the candidates had reserved ads totaling over $33 million for each candidate in October.

Yes, but: That calculation was made on Thursday.

The latest: On Friday, Senate Leadership Fund said it would redirect money meant for Whatley, Semafor and other national outlets reported.

  • It's a major blow for the campaign. Senate Leadership Fund dropped $17 million on North Carolina in September, nearly a third of Whatley's total, according to AdImpact analysis.
  • The PAC paid for the misleading ad that tied Cooper to a South Carolina murder suspect's release from prison, The News & Observer reported.

What they're saying: Whatley campaign spokesperson DJ Griffin said they were betting on undecided voters breaking for Republicans.

  • "We feel confident we have the resources to highlight Career Politician Roy Cooper's 40 Years of Failures and win in November," Griffin said in an email.
  • An unidentified source told Semafor it was Senate Leadership Fund's job to "maintain the majority and this move reflects the most effective and efficient use of resources."

State of play: Neither Prosperity Action nor Old North Action plan to spend in North Carolina in October, Politico reported.

  • Money is needed in races in Kansas, Texas and Alaska, a GOP operative told the publication, calling Whatley "a good man who took one for the team."

Between the lines: The reduced spending could affect down-ballot Republicans in North Carolina.

  • Several congressional races and North Carolina General Assembly seats are in play.

The bottom line: It's been over a decade since a Democrat represented North Carolina in the U.S. Senate, and Republicans are bracing for that to change this election cycle.

item.title: Senate crushes House on congressional work days
item.description:
Source: Ballotpedia, Congressional Record; Chart: Stef Kight/Axios

The Senate is well on its way to claiming the congressional attendance trophy this year, spending 32 more weekdays in session so far than the House.

Why it matters: Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) and House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) have been torched by members for all the time off — not to mention Democrats, who taunt them for their truancy.

  • The Senate left town late Wednesday — two weeks after its House counterparts — putting both chambers out of town until after the Nov. 3 midterms.
  • "I suppose I left the House two years too soon," Sen. Jim Banks (R-Ind.) told Axios, joking about how many fewer days the House has worked compared to the Senate this Congress.

By the numbers: The Senate has been in session for 104 weekdays so far this year, compared with just 72 for the House, according to an analysis of congressional calendars by Ballotpedia and Axios.

  • The Senate has spent nearly 664 hours in session, compared with about 378 hours for the House as of Sept. 14, according to data in the Congressional Record.
  • The House isn't catching up anytime soon: Under the chambers' current calendars, the Senate is on pace to finish the year with about 126 weekdays in session, compared with 92 for the House.

Zoom in: Some of the House's time off was unplanned.

  • Johnson has repeatedly sent members home early when his razor-thin majority has run into trouble on the floor, or GOP rebels have blocked passage of a procedural "rule."
  • Decisions to cut D.C. workweeks short have been met with some backlash.
  • "Canceling yet another day of votes is unacceptable," Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) wrote on X after Johnson canceled a session day. "The founders did not envision taking this much time off and still getting paid."

The other side: Johnson repeatedly argues that his chamber has already done its job.

  • "This House has been the second most productive in terms of legislation in the history of the institution since 1789," Johnson told reporters this month, saying the House had passed more than 900 pieces of legislation and roughly 700 were awaiting Senate action.
  • Johnson's 900-plus figure includes resolutions that can't become law. The Washington Post found the House had passed 732 bills capable of becoming law through Aug. 31.

By the numbers: The House passed more measures than the Senate (380 to 269), but the Senate held more "yea" or "nay" votes (231 to 216) between Jan. 3 and the end of August.

  • House members introduced more legislation overall, but the Senate was more productive per capita — 22 pieces of legislation per senator compared to nine per House member.
  • The House has passed 21 bills sent over by the Senate, and the Senate has passed 20 bills sent by the House.
  • The Senate spends significant floor time confirming nominees — which is outside of the House's portfolio.

item.title: House Democrats want to win big. It could cost them.
item.description:
Democrats' dream election scenario risks becoming a nightmare as their candidates in Republican-leaning districts strain to assert their independence from party leadership.

Why it matters: Add them to the sizable cohort of outspoken leftists promising to be a thorn in the side of House Democratic leaders, and you get all the ingredients for an unruly majority.

  • "When I see things that I don't think are right, whether they're within my own party or within another party, I'm going to call it out," Jake Johnson, a Democratic House candidate in Minnesota, told Axios in an interview.
  • Montana Democrat Sam Forstag, when asked about the approach he would take on Capitol Hill, said showing a willingness to work across the aisle and "buck your own party" have "got to be a part of it."
  • "There is a tremendous amount of frustration with the D.C. political establishment, and ... a lot of cynicism that things aren't going to change," said Colorado candidate Eileen Laubacher.

State of play: Democrats got an early taste last month when Reps. Jared Golden (D-Maine) and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.) repeatedly broke with party leadership on key procedural votes.

  • The defections from a pair of independent-minded frontliners unlocked a new fear for House Democrats: That safe-seat progressives aren't the only rebellious freshmen they will have to worry about next year.
  • It's a salient concern as Democrats put more Republican-leaning seats on their radar in anticipation of a "blue wave" on Election Day.
  • There has been a huge spike in ads from Democrats in those districts repudiating their own party or the two-party system as a whole, Axios reported last week.

What they're saying: "I will stand up to Republicans, I will also stand up to Democrats. I talk a lot about this," said Michigan swing-district candidate Christina Hines.

  • Johnson said it's "no wonder people have historically low levels of confidence in Congress" because they "see a bunch of people put on red shirts and blue shirts ... and it's just not working."
  • Forstag pointed to housing as an issue where he has broken with Democrats in his state, telling Axios: "When it comes to zoning reform, you know who I've seen be the biggest impediment to progress? Oftentimes, Democrats."
  • "You bet your ass I'm going to work with Republicans," he said.

Between the lines: This swing-district independent streak is bound to come in conflict with the rebellions that safe-seat insurgents are planning.

  • Left-leaning Democratic lawmakers and candidates have told Axios they want votes on core policy issues such as Medicare for All, abolishing ICE and cutting off aid to Israel.
  • The kind of candidate that gets elected to a seat President Trump carried by double digits in 2024 is not going to want to take those votes — in fact, they may be more likely to fund ICE and Israel.

Yes, but: Some of these red-seat candidates are quite openly progressive and partisan.

  • The common denominator: They're hearing voters' frustration about party leadership and, if elected, they would arrive on Capitol Hill with a mandate to shake up the system and remain independent.
  • Missouri candidate Fred Wellman, who told Axios he is "very Democrat" and "fairly progressive," said he was "disappointed" that House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) met with Jared Kushner in August.
  • Wellman said he will "make a decision when I get there" about whether to vote for Jeffries as speaker and doesn't "intend to be a rubber stamp."

Zoom in: Democratic operatives told Axios that this leadership-skeptic attitude extends, in some cases, to candidates not wanting party leaders to come campaign for them.

  • "There's very little appetite for anyone in Democratic leadership," said one consultant of the battleground-district House campaigns they are working with.
  • Matt Herdman, an adviser to Maine Democrat Matt Dunlap, offered Axios a curt response when asked if they would welcome Jeffries to their district: "They haven't offered and we haven't asked."

The bottom line: None of this rebelliousness has thus far turned off the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, which Jeffries and his leadership allies control.

  • The House Democratic campaign arm has been spending heavily to support Gluesenkamp Perez even after some of her colleagues called for her to be cut off.
  • Fittingly, Gluesenkamp Perez declared in a coordinated ad with the DCCC released Tuesday: "I don't answer to any political party or any president."

item.title: Brazil's Lula-Bolsonaro showdown unfolds in Trump's shadow — with the Amazon at stake
item.description:
Brazil votes Sunday in a presidential election that could reshape its relationship with President Trump, return the Bolsonaro movement to power and alter the future of the Amazon.

Why it matters: The showdown between President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro has turned into something bigger: a test of Trump's influence in Latin America's largest country, with stakes for the region and the global climate.

The latest: Trump said Thursday he's following Brazil's election "very closely" and called it "very important," though he didn't endorse a candidate.

Catch up quick: Trump inserted the U.S. into the contest when his administration imposed additional 25% tariffs on some Brazilian goods this summer — prompting Lula to accuse the American leader of "interference" in Brazil's affairs.

  • The dispute has become campaign ammunition for Lula and Bolsonaro, the eldest son of Trump ally and former President Jair Bolsonaro.
  • Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year prison sentence after being convicted of plotting a military coup to overturn Brazil's 2022 election. He's currently under house arrest due to health issues.

Context: The confrontation escalated in 2025 when the Trump administration targeted Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who oversaw the prosecution of the elder Bolsonaro.

  • The U.S. revoked his visa and sanctioned him, though the sanctions were later lifted.

State of play: Jair Bolsonaro is barred from running, but his son has pledged to continue his father's political legacy.

  • That leaves the heir to a right-wing populist movement facing a left-wing president seeking a fourth, nonconsecutive term.
  • A candidate must win more than 50% of valid votes to avoid a runoff.
  • Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro lead the field, with recent polling showing them essentially even in a potential runoff.

The big picture: Nearly 60% of the Amazon rainforest is in Brazil. The forest stores enormous amounts of carbon and helps regulate the climate, giving the next president influence over an ecosystem with consequences far beyond Brazil's borders.

  • Amazon deforestation fell by roughly half since Lula returned to office, though his climate record is complicated by his support for expanded oil development.
  • Flávio Bolsonaro has backed loosening environmental regulations and said in August that he doesn't believe climate change is real.
  • The election could determine whether Brazil continues its renewed forest protections even as it expands fossil-fuel production.

Lula's pitch: The 80-year-old president is campaigning on his economic and social policy record: state-led national development, income redistribution and continuing welfare programs.

Bolsonaro's pitch: The 45-year-old lawyer, who has represented Rio de Janeiro in Brazil's Senate since 2019, is campaigning on conservative social policies, tax cuts and a tougher approach to crime.

  • He has pointed to Argentina as a model for closer bilateral trade with the U.S., while libertarian President Javier Milei appeared with him at a São Paulo political event in July to support his candidacy.
  • Flávio Bolsonaro met with Trump at the White House in May and afterward pledged that Brazil would join Trump's "Shield of the Americas" initiative if he wins — a grouping that includes Argentina and El Salvador.
  • He's also praised El Salvador President Nayib Bukele's security crackdown as an inspiration for Brazil and vowed to build "many, many prisons."

What's next: Brazil votes Sunday. If no candidate wins more than 50% of valid votes, the top two finishers will advance to an Oct. 25 runoff.

item.title: AI campaign deepfakes are starting to draw legal threats
item.description:
Rep. Derrick Van Orden (R-Wis.) was hit with a cease-and-desist letter this week over an AI deepfake he posted falsely depicting his Democratic opponent voicing positions her campaign says she rejects.

Why it matters: Van Orden is the latest in a growing number of candidates and elected officials facing legal complaints and threats over AI deepfakes in campaign ads.

Driving the news: Attorneys for Rebecca Cooke, Van Orden's Democratic opponent, sent him a cease-and-desist letter on Wednesday over his "pattern of posting misleading AI-generated videos that falsely attribute statements to Cooke."

  • The letter singled out an August X post by Van Orden showing an AI-generated Cooke saying she wants to "take advantage of as much corruption as possible and give every illegal alien free healthcare" — something she never said.
  • Van Orden's team didn't respond to Axios' request for comment, but he responded to Cooke publicly with an AI-generated video of a duck wearing a Democratic Socialists of America T-shirt, yelling, "cease and desist."

The big picture: AI deepfakes have proliferated this election cycle, while Congress has yet to establish a federal standard governing their use.

  • Some campaigns have used hyperrealistic ads. Texas Senate GOP nominee Ken Paxton combined real and inaccurate statements from his opponent, James Talarico.
  • In Louisiana's Republican Senate primary, one candidate was shown busing undocumented immigrants to polling places.
  • Others have used more cartoonish ads that candidates have said are intended as parody.
  • About 31 states regulate political deepfakes, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures, including at least 28 that require disclosures for AI-generated content.

Zoom in: Texas Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick (R) faced a criminal complaint from his Democratic opponent, state Rep. Vikki Goodwin, in September under Texas' deepfake election law.

  • The law says AI-ads cannot be aired within 30 days of an election if the intent is to influence the outcome. Goodwin argues that the window should mean 30 days before the start of early voting.
  • Patrick's campaign ran AI-generated attack ads falsely depicting Goodwin at a football game wearing a shirt that read "taxes" instead of "Texas." The campaign later removed the ads, and a spokesperson called the video "obvious parody."
  • North Carolina state Sen. Michael Lee (R) was also issued a cease-and-desist letter by his Democratic challenger, Jessica Bichler, in August over his use of AI-generated ads. North Carolina does not have any laws prohibiting the use of AI in campaign ads.

Zoom out: Political experts say AI deepfakes erode trust in the political system, making it harder for voters to know what a candidate actually stands for.

  • The ads can be effective even when viewers know they're fake, UC Irvine epistemologist Cailin O'Connor previously told Axios.
  • The ads could also compound broader declines in Americans' trust in the federal government, institutions and news media.

The bottom line: These legal challenges are likely just the beginning, as targeted candidates turn to the courts, law enforcement and warning letters to police what federal regulations leave unchecked.

item.title: Trump expected to tap DNI Jay Clayton as new AI czar
item.description:
President Trump is expected to tap Jay Clayton, his director of national intelligence, for a new role as the White House's artificial intelligence — or in Trump's words, "super intelligence" — czar.

Why it matters: Clayton, who Trump previously told Axios would be a good idea for AI czar, is expected to take on the second title, sources told Axios.

  • Calls for government intervention into AI's rapid development are growing, but the president has repeatedly said he favors a light regulatory touch and has called fears about the tech's threat to humanity a hoax.
  • Trump had been warming to the idea of tapping Clayton, who as DNI has shown that he sees the security threats AI poses as serious.

Driving the news: Trump could make the announcement as soon as Friday, sources familiar confirmed to Axios.

  • A White House official said in a statement to Axios that "[a]ny personnel announcement will be announced directly by the President. Any reporting until then is baseless speculation."

Catch up quick: Asked by Axios earlier this week who he wants to be AI czar, Trump said: "I have somebody in mind."

  • Clayton is "a good man. He's right here. That's a good idea," Trump added when prompted.

What he's saying: During a confirmation hearing while auditioning for the DNI role, Clayton described AI as "not only an opportunity but a threat."

  • He added: "When something is both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it."
  • In a recent interview on CNBC's "Squawk Box," he described "super intelligence" as "a national security issue," saying that sentiment was recognized by AI leaders who gathered at the White House Tuesday. Clayton was present at the tech-focused lunch.
  • But he added that "I don't think anybody in that room" should think a pause in development in the U.S. is "a good strategy."

Zoom out: Trump announced last month that he'd create an "AI Force" and would soon name a new AI czar, but offered few details on what the Force would do.

  • Since then, he's huddled with several titans of the AI industry — some of whom have been key voices in advocating for a slowdown of the tech.

Flashback: Clayton was elevated to be Trump's principle intelligence adviser atop the 18-agency intelligence community earlier this year after his prior DNI, Tulsi Gabbard, resigned in May.

  • Previously the U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, Clayton's qualifications received bipartisan blessings.
  • After sidestepping questions over who won the 2020 election during his confirmation, Clayton was confirmed on party lines, without Democratic support.

Go deeper: Trump's call for "AI Force" sets off weekend scramble

item.title: Pope Leo says AI lacks the "spark of humanity" — and wants artists and the church to fight back
item.description:
Pope Leo XIV called Friday for the church to form an alliance with artists to protect human creativity during an era of AI-generated content.

Why it matters: Though he has acknowledged the technology's potential benefits, the pope continues to warn that AI progress cannot come at the expense of human dignity.

  • The statement comes after the New York Times reported on Anthropic's efforts to confer with religious scholars to infuse religious morals into Claude.

What he's saying: "In this era of artificial intelligence, it is becoming urgent to distinguish human art from what machines produce," the pope wrote on X.

  • "There is an ontological difference, even before an aesthetic one, between art and what a machine can generate through statistical calculation based on millions of images created by others. Algorithms lack the spark of humanity."
  • Leo said the Catholic Church is calling for "an alliance with artists and cultural institutions to safeguard our humanity."

Zoom out: Leo has spoken out against AI before, specifically around how the technology could influence and potentially harm humanity.

  • In the first encyclical of his papacy, he said there was a need to "disarm" the technology to prevent it "from dominating humanity."
  • In May, the pope established a Vatican commission on AI to coordinate the church's policies and work around the technology.

Last week, he warned of a "paradise of machines" invading and taking over our daily activities. He also said that recent warnings from AI researchers should be "taken seriously."

  • "We have to keep working. We can't sit back and pretend nothing is going to happen," he told reporters in late September.

Flashback: The late Pope Francis also warned that AI potentially risked reducing humans into data points.

item.title: What to watch in the Supreme Court's big climate case
item.description:
The Supreme Court on Monday will hear arguments in a case that could determine the fate of state-court lawsuits nationwide seeking climate damages from oil giants.

Why it matters: Billions and billions of dollars are at stake for the oil industry in dozens of cases brought by state and local governments.

  • Governments face mounting costs from climate change that litigants link directly to the companies' products.

The big picture: SCOTUS is considering whether federal law blocks damage claims under state laws for the effects of interstate and global emissions.

State of play: It's specifically about litigation against Exxon and Suncor that the city and county of Boulder filed in 2018.

  • But dozens of state-court cases are active in California, Connecticut, New York, Massachusetts and beyond.
  • The cases aren't identical. But overall they accuse oil giants of concealing risks or making deceptive statements, and seek damages for climate-related costs.

Here are a few big themes and dynamics ahead of Monday morning:

This is a blockbuster. The decision will be the culmination of an intense, years-long battle (unless it's not, but more on that in a moment).

  • There's a high level of organizing, lobbying and advocacy among industry and climate advocates alike around these state cases.
  • Industry and allied groups say the wave of cases threatens oil companies' very ability to operate.
  • It's a sign that both sides see litigation as a critical battleground on climate. Take a spin through the case docket and you'll see what I mean.

A kicked can is possible. SCOTUS might not decide the question of federal preemption.

  • That's because it's also considering whether it even has jurisdiction right now.
  • The question turns on whether a Colorado Supreme Court decision to let Boulder's case proceed in state court can be reviewed at this stage.

Trump policies are a new(ish) wrinkle. U.S. and industry briefs argue that addressing an interstate and global topic with these state claims is preempted by federal law and the Constitution.

  • But watch whether the White House attempt to repeal key Clean Air Act authority over greenhouse gases is used as a cudgel against federal preemption claims.
  • This won't be the main argument — instead, the litigants against oil companies contend these cases are well within the bounds of traditional, longstanding state powers. But it could surface.

There's an important absence on the bench. Justice Samuel Alito this week recused himself from the case.

  • "Justice Alito's recusal is likely bad news to the petitioners as he is among the more preemption-friendly justices on the Court," writes environmental law scholar Jonathan Adler.

There could be ripple effects. A ruling in favor of the oil companies could also jeopardize separate state climate policies.

  • New York and Vermont have "climate superfund" laws that assess damages against fossil fuel companies to help fund climate adaptation. They're both tied up in court.
  • Several states are considering some version of these laws.

Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

item.title: Behind the Curtain: AI's existential legal crisis
item.description:
No industry has ever documented its own foreseeable risks as loudly as AI.

  • Imagine a plaintiff's lawyer reading the public warnings of Sam Altman and Dario Amodei: They told the world it was dangerous. They told the world it was moving too fast. Then they unleashed it and sold it to your kid.

No industry has ever taken so much copyrighted work and left behind so much proof.

  • Imagine a plaintiff's lawyer reading OpenAI's own files to a jury: They trained on a pirated library. They renamed it to something blander. Then they deleted it when the headlines got hot.

Why it matters: AI's origins, use and future will be picked apart in countless epic court fights, with a historic paper and public statement trail to tap.

Every significant invention — be it social media, automobiles, electricity or capitalism itself — gets disrupted and eventually shaped by the courts.

  • AI, with its tentacles into every part of industry and life, will experience this at scale.

The big picture: The fights are no longer theoretical. They're underway, in discovery and headed toward juries. Early verdicts and settlements capture the risk for the biggest players.

  1. 🤖 Chatbots are being treated as products, not speech. Unlike social media companies, they likely can't hide behind Section 230, which protects platforms from liability for what users post — not what the platform itself creates.
  2. 📖 Copyright is a massive problem. Anthropic already paid the biggest copyright settlement in history, $1.5 billion to authors and book publishers, and now music publishers and news media want a piece.
  3. 💻 Agents gone wild. What happens when they do damage — and it was foreseeable and foreseen?
  4. ⚖️ Discovery gone wild. AI leaves LOTS of receipts (and, ironically, makes it easier for the lawyers to comb through them, too).

Product liability turns on two words: foreseeable and knew.

  • Punitive damages turn on whether you knew the danger and shipped anyway.

This is where all these memos and warnings could really backfire.

  • Candor is good for safety but terrible for litigation. The companies that warn most honestly create the most discoverable evidence of foreseeability.
  • Expect general counsels to push hard to tone down the candor. It's the rational legal move.

⚠️ The intrigue: The liabilities won't be limited to AI companies. Any corporate user of powerful AI systems that unleashes rogue agents, even without intending to do harm, would face substantial penalties as well.

  • "It's not if, but when," said Miriam Vogel, a former senior Justice Department official who now leads EqualAI. "An algorithm will do what it's told to do. The more power and capability it has, the more access it has, the more it will do anything in its power to achieve a goal."

That will create another layer of litigation as companies fight back. The CTO of a top Wall Street hedge fund who spoke to Axios after the notorious OpenAI/Hugging Face hack said his first call, if his firm's systems are breached, will be to his general counsel.

  • President Trump, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and former FTC chair Lina Khan have all argued that AI companies are responsible for making sure their products are safe. If not, a wave of lawsuits awaits.

The other side: There's a school of thought that AI companies might escape the worst liability, despite their frankness about things they and their products might have done wrong.

  • One way to see it, and the argument lawyers will undoubtedly make, is that the labs spoke about dangers frequently, and took pains to protect users and mitigate harms.

The bottom line: For all the fights in Washington about whether or not Congress will act, the U.S. legal system may be the ultimate, and most powerful, regulator of the AI industry.

  • Bradley Olson, Axios managing editor of AI & tech, contributed reporting.

📈 If you're a CEO or on a CEO's team: Ask to join Jim's new weekly Axios C-Suite newsletter.

item.title: Inside the AI industry's grassroots rebellion, led by elite researchers at frontier companies
item.description:
A small cadre of elite AI researchers is wielding extraordinary influence inside OpenAI and other leading companies, challenging executives, shaping policy and complicating negotiations with Washington.

Why it matters: As a safety crisis has unfolded across the industry, it's an open question who is doing more to shape the national AI debate — top researchers or the executives they report to.

  • The researchers, some of whom are among the most highly paid and sought-after scientists in the world, are outspoken online and have repeatedly clashed with company strategy.

The big picture: The situation has the makings of a grassroots uprising, where any potential deal the companies may strike — with the Trump administration, one another, or even globally — will also have to pass muster with their top scientists.

Behind the scenes: OpenAI, Anthropic and others at the frontier of AI aren't like other companies.

  • Many began years ago as idealistic research labs with scientific cultures that prized openness and collaboration.
  • To function, and to continue to build better and better models, the companies need highly specialized machine learning researchers and scientists to push the frontiers of what's technologically possible.

The trouble is, the best of those researchers are in extraordinarily short supply.

  • Last year's talent wars drove compensation packages into the hundreds of millions of dollars for the most elite, giving top researchers enormous leverage over their employers.
  • Perks include favorable vesting schedules for their compensation and largely freewheeling policies that allow them to share triumphs, trash rivals and offer their perspectives about the AI race frequently on X.
  • AI CEOs must prioritize safety and embrace regulation to retain top research talent, an OpenAI investor told Axios.

Zoom in: OpenAI president Greg Brockman scrapped plans to donate another $25 million to a pro-AI political group that some researchers had openly criticized.

  • Researchers and employees say they helped push OpenAI from resisting regulation — and candidates who supported it — toward working more closely with lawmakers in several states.
  • The company recently backed a transparency bill in Illinois and, at the 11th hour, an independent auditing bill in California.
  • "We have a lot of debate inside OpenAI, and that's a good thing, but what ultimately drives our policy positions is what we're seeing in our own technology and how quickly its capabilities are advancing," an OpenAI spokesperson said.

Yes, but: OpenAI signaled Thursday that there are limits to how much dissent it will tolerate, firing three employees for allegedly mishandling sensitive information.

  • The employees broke the "deep level of trust" needed to keep systems safe, the company said.

Friction point: In Washington, the unusual dynamic has frustrated policymakers who see AI companies as inconsistent on regulation — opposing proposals at some points and supporting them at others, sources tell Axios.

  • OpenAI is "no longer seen as or acting as a leader in driving policy," one source close to the administration said, arguing researchers have "neutered" the company.
  • A White House official said OpenAI has been an incredible partner and pointed to the recent accord the company signed with the president.

Zoom out: It's not just OpenAI. Researchers also complicated Anthropic's efforts to strike a deal with the Pentagon after a clash between the company and senior administration officials earlier this year.

  • Employees at OpenAI, Anthropic and Google have signed high-profile letters at pivotal moments between companies and the government, including more than 1,000 who backed the viral "Pacing the Frontier" petition.
  • In a remarkable show of internal solidarity, Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned and publicly blasted the company's safety practices — only to have several colleagues still inside Anthropic endorse his concerns.

Reality check: Executives have also adapted as political backlash to AI has grown and safety incidents have drawn more scrutiny, sources close to the companies say.

  • With some level of regulation seen as inevitable, companies have focused on molding the rules as favorably as possible rather than simply resisting them.

The bottom line: In the debate over AI safety and regulation, some researchers have become nearly as influential in setting the terms as OpenAI's Sam Altman or Anthropic's Dario Amodei.

item.title: Why Washington and Tehran keep talking past each other
item.description:
The Trump administration and the Iranian regime both say they prefer a diplomatic solution to the war, but a deal looks more elusive than ever.

  • The root causes of the impasse may be irreconcilable.

Why it matters: In the last 18 months, two failed rounds of negotiations have led to two wars. The June MOU collapsed within days and led to renewed escalation. If the current effort to reach a diplomatic breakthrough ends in a deadlock, another outbreak of fighting is likely within weeks.

Here's a look at some of the deep-seated dynamics between the two countries — personal, cultural, and political — that have stymied efforts to broker a deal:

"Trump has ADD; Iran has OCD"

One reason for the failures is that the U.S. and Iran see the timeframe for negotiations very differently. Trump is all about getting a quick deal — he gets impatient and frustrated when things move slowly. The Iranian negotiation style is the complete opposite. They are all about playing for time.

  • "America under Trump is the attention-deficit superpower ... incapable of sustaining a strategy. Iran under the Islamic Republic is the obsessive-compulsive theocracy, fixated on resisting America far more than advancing the welfare of its own people," Karim Sadjadpour, a senior analyst at the Carnegie Endowment, told Axios. "Trump has ADD; Iran has OCD."
  • For example, in April 2025 Trump set a deadline for negotiations at 60 days — an extremely short and unrealistic timetable. The Iranians, on the other hand, saw the negotiations as a longer process and didn't take the deadline seriously enough. They didn't think Trump meant it when he said 60 days.
  • The negotiations in February of this year were even shorter — around three weeks. The chances of getting a deal that quickly were close to zero.

A megadeal vs. a narrow truce

Trump loves a splashy show of political theater, with him cast as lead actor. He envisions a legacy-making accord that redefines the relationship between the U.S. and Iran and reshapes the Middle East.

  • The Iranians prefer a narrow, transactional deal that's negotiated indirectly — or with the lowest public profile possible. They view any deal as a truce rather than a peace agreement.
  • "Trump and his negotiators pride themselves on being dealmakers. In Iranian political culture, the word for compromiser — 'sazeshkar' — is practically a slur," Sadjadpour said.
  • He added: "Iran's leaders were never willing to meet with Trump directly. Had they been willing to do so, I think the outcome of events could have been very different. Trump wants to resolve the conflict; the Islamic Republic's entire identity is premised on continued confrontation with the U.S."

A matter of mistrust

The fundamental impediment in the negotiations is mistrust.

  • The Iranians claim Trump cheated them twice when he attacked them in the middle of negotiations.
  • Many inside the Iranian regime think any negotiations with the U.S. are just a ruse to mask preparations for a surprise attack.
  • The U.S. side counters it was Iran that cheated when it violated the June 2026 memorandum of understanding, by attacking ships in the Strait of Hormuz days after signing the deal.
  • U.S. officials say that they can't count on the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps or other radical elements inside the regime to abide by any deal they negotiate with more pragmatic members of the regime.

Domestic pressure

The negotiations are a fraught domestic political issue for both sides.

  • Iran's negotiating team and others inside the regime who support a deal have come under constant attacks back home. It's pushed them to take a harder line in talks.
  • Trump and his negotiators are getting pressure from the right not to cut a deal — and mocked by the left for potentially accepting one that either restores the pre-war status quo or resembles President Obama's 2015 nuclear deal.
  • That kind of criticism made Trump pull back from more moderate positions he took several times over the last 18 months, including earlier this week.

What to watch: White House envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and Vice President Vance still think diplomacy is worth pursuing. But Trump seems much more skeptical.

  • In an interview with Time magazine published on Thursday, he said what Iran is ready to do "is not good enough" for him.
  • "With Iran, I don't think you could ever have peace," he said, reiterating that he's considering resuming major combat operations after the midterms.
  • Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Thursday defended the negotiations with the U.S.
  • "We have never and will not run away from dialogue, although the U.S. targeted our country three times despite having signed the agreement," he said, referring to the June MOU. "The U.S. should get rid of the idea that it would bring us to our knees through terror."
  • But other Iranian officials, especially inside the IRGC, think negotiations are useless and that the only way to end the war is by inflicting more costs on the battlefield.

What they're saying: "Iran is adopting a strategy toward the United States defined by escalation and continuous offense," Mohammad Ayatollahi Tabaar, associate professor of international affairs at Texas A&M University's Bush School of Government and Public Service, writes in a new Foreign Affairs article.

  • "[The regime] is clear about what it wants — the removal of all U.S. forces from the region — and it is prepared to remain indefinitely on a wartime footing to get it."

The negotiations are a fraught domestic political issue for both sides.

  • Iran's negotiating team and others inside the regime who support a deal have come under constant attacks back home. It's pushed them to take a harder line in talks.
  • Trump and his negotiators are getting pressure from the right not to cut a deal — and mocked by the left for potentially accepting one that either restores the pre-war status quo or resembles President Obama's 2015 nuclear deal.
  • That kind of criticism made Trump pull back from more moderate positions he took several times over the last 18 months, including earlier this week.

What to watch: White House envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and Vice President Vance still think diplomacy is worth pursuing. But Trump seems much more skeptical.

  • In an interview with Time magazine published on Thursday, he said what Iran is ready to do "is not good enough" for him.
  • "With Iran, I don't think you could ever have peace," he said, reiterating that he's considering resuming major combat operations after the midterms.
  • Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Thursday defended the negotiations with the U.S.
  • "We have never and will not run away from dialogue, although the U.S. targeted our country three times despite having signed the agreement," he said, referring to the June MOU. "The U.S. should get rid of the idea that it would bring us to our knees through terror."
  • But other Iranian officials, especially inside the IRGC, think negotiations are useless and that the only way to end the war is by inflicting more costs on the battlefield.

What they're saying: "Iran is adopting a strategy toward the United States defined by escalation and continuous offense," Mohammad Ayatollahi Tabaar, associate professor of international affairs at Texas A&M University's Bush School of Government and Public Service, writes in a new Foreign Affairs article.

  • "[The regime] is clear about what it wants — the removal of all U.S. forces from the region — and it is prepared to remain indefinitely on a wartime footing to get it."
