item.title: "Strange bedfellows": Bernie Sanders, Florida Dems and a benchmark $250k donation
item.description:
MIAMI — Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders is sending the Florida Democratic Party $250,000. It's a relative pittance in the Sunshine State — but the check signals a big political shift.

Why it matters: The state party's moderate leaders have resisted the rising tide of democratic socialists elevated by Sanders for years. But political changes and financial need have brought the two together like never before:

  1. The Florida Democratic Party is essentially broke after decades of being out of power, and national establishment Democratic organizations have so far refused to help.
  2. Florida state Rep Angie Nixon, who joined the Democratic Socialists of America this summer, is the state party's U.S. Senate nominee. Sanders endorsed her and has long wanted to help, an aide said.

Zoom in: Despite being vastly outraised and outspent in Florida, Nixon and Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Jolly are stubbornly close in polling to their respective Republican opponents, Sen. Ashley Moody and Rep. Byron Donalds.

  • Until now, national Democrats have been hesitant to spend in Florida due to years of soul-crushing defeats —especially at the hands of President Trump and Gov. Ron DeSantis — that made the state and its 10 expensive media markets look like a bad investment.
  • This year, with Republican fortunes sagging nationwide, Texas, Ohio, Iowa and Alaska look more promising for Democrats.

That could change soon. Nixon told a liberal podcaster Thursday that the chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, New York Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, held a fundraiser for her.

  • Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), whom Nixon called out last week for not helping, also might make money available.
  • "Folks are a little gun-shy because, unfortunately, Vice President [Kamala] Harris lost as a Black woman. And so people are being very hesitant in terms of funding Black women, especially in the South," Nixon told MS NOW's "Clock It with Symone & Eugene."

Behind the scenes: Florida Democratic Party chair Nikki Fried has been constantly working national donors for money, allies say, but she never asked Sanders for help because of their ideological differences and resistance within the state party.

  • Socialists — and Sanders' associated views — have long been regarded as political liabilities in a state where so many Hispanic voters hailed from countries associated with leftist violence.
  • But when Sanders signaled he was ready to give to a "victory fund" that joins the state party and Nixon's campaign, Fried didn't stand in the way.
  • "Angie's going to turn out our base," Fried privately told skeptical allies in the party. "Every dollar that helps Angie, helps Jolly and helps the candidates down ballot."

Friction point: Establishment Democrats are divided between those who don't want to be associated with Sanders and those who wanted him to give more of his $23 million campaign fund than just $250,000.

  • "That's it? He should send more," said Florida Rep. Lois Frankel, who has been critical of Sanders and doesn't agree with Sanders' and Nixon's criticisms of Israel.
  • "Republicans are going to kill us for taking Bernie socialist money and we're not even getting enough of it," one Democratic candidate groused. "But yeah, strange bedfellows."
  • Said Javier Fernandez, a Democratic mayor of the city of South Miami: "The more we rally around Bernie, the more we hurt our long-term prospects."
  • "It's a Faustian bargain: The party captures the energy and dynamism of the Bernie/DSA that are trying to use the party, but it compromises core values of moderate and progressive Democrats and puts us further out of step with the views of mainstream voters."

The big picture: The Democratic Party is evolving as progressives and socialist-aligned candidates and activists energize its base.

  • Nationwide, 65% of Democrats now have a favorable view of socialism, according to a Gallup survey released last week that also found support rising among independents.
  • Nixon is the Democratic engine drawing enthusiastic crowds in Florida. Her rallies double as organizational events to harness volunteers to knock on doors, make phone-bank calls or volunteer. She also has a notable social media presence and a stable of influencers.
  • It's a stark contrast with Jolly's low-key candidacy, which has a small social-media footprint and events.

Between the lines: After some initial tension, Nixon's campaign is aligned with the state party, which is providing additional organizational support.

  • Statewide, the state party reports an army of 6,000 volunteers who helped Democrats flip 46 seats in legislative, school-board and local-government races across Florida in two years.
  • Florida Democrats are now keeping pace with the GOP in voter registration gains.
  • Sanders has sent his staff and organizers to Florida to help Nixon with literature, texting and phone-banking.

Yes, but: Florida Republicans still have far more registered voters, an edge of more than 1.5 million. And the Florida GOP has a well-oiled turnout machine and a stable of political pros who have consistently helped keep the state reliably red.

  • "We don't lose Florida," one of them said, noting Moody and Donalds are marginally ahead of Nixon and Jolly in most polls.
  • Still, there are jitters in the GOP as gas prices rise along with interest rates and the real estate market cools.
  • "I'm not going to say Angie or Jolly are going to win," said one GOP consultant. "It's hard to see a DSA candidate winning a general [election], but could I see a world where she turns out the base and falls short but Jolly benefits from it and ekes it out? Nobody knows."

What they're saying: Nixon's campaign manager, Eunic Ortiz, said the money from Sanders helps, but big money is less salient nowadays.

  • Republicans' "billionaire donors will likely outspend us, but we know we will out-organize them," Ortiz said. "We're going to win with people on the ground, neighbors talking to neighbors, and the kind of energy and excitement money can't buy."
  • "Did we see a world where Bernie led the way in getting national money to Florida? No," said an ally of Fried's. "But national donors are starting to give to Florida. And Bernie was the first nod the nation is paying attention."

Axios' Holly Otterbein contributed to this story.

item.title: "We're not asking for charity": Wikimedia CEO calls out AI for unpaid data use
item.description:
Wikipedia is starting to feel the effects of the AI-driven shift in how people find information, with page views falling 8% in the latest year, new Wikimedia Foundation CEO Bernadette Meehan told Axios.

Why it matters: Wikipedia is a crucial source of information for AI models, but those same models increasingly allow people to get Wikipedia-derived information without ever visiting the site — potentially threatening the ecosystem that keeps the online encyclopedia running.

Driving the news: Wikipedia page views declined 8% in 2025, and while the drop wasn't unexpected, "that doesn't mean that we're sort of starry-eyed about it and not concerned about it," Meehan said.

Follow the money: The problem is that even though generative AI systems rely heavily on Wikipedia's vast trove of human-created information, some companies won't pay for it, she said.

  • Wikimedia has a program that charges large-scale commercial users for reliable, high-volume access to its data. Publicly disclosed enterprise customers, whose payments make up 10% of the organization's operating expenses, include Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Meta, Perplexity and others.
  • OpenAI and Anthropic, two of the largest makers of generative AI models, aren't among Wikimedia's publicly disclosed enterprise customers. Meehan noted that Wikimedia has other agreements that aren't publicly disclosed and declined to identify those companies.
  • OpenAI and Anthropic both declined to comment.

What they're saying: Meehan, a former U.S. ambassador to Chile who took over Wikimedia's top job in January, said the reception from big technology companies has been mixed.

  • Some have embraced the idea that companies benefiting from Wikipedia should help sustain it. Others, she said, have acknowledged what Wikimedia considers excessive use of its data but declined to pay for enterprise access.
  • "We're not asking for charity," Meehan said.

Between the lines: There's an unusual economic tension here: Wikipedia makes its content freely available and has no intention of changing that, leaving it with limited leverage over AI companies that don't want to pay.

The big picture: Traffic matters to Wikimedia for reasons that go well beyond bragging rights for being one of the most popular destinations on the internet.

  • Roughly 80% of Wikimedia's operating budget comes from small donations, many prompted by banners shown to visitors to its site.
  • Readers also provide the pipeline for future Wikipedia editors. "If less readers are coming, that's less conversion to editors," Meehan said.

Ironically, Wikipedia has arguably never been more valuable to the broader information ecosystem.

  • "We're the backbone," Meehan said when asked about Wikipedia's importance to AI knowledge engines.

Meanwhile, Meehan is drawing a distinction between AI using Wikipedia and AI creating Wikipedia.

  • AI remains controversial among Wikipedia's volunteer communities, which set their own rules, but it is already being used for tasks such as translation, finding broken links and helping new editors spot problems with their contributions.

Meehan sees a clear boundary, though: AI should assist Wikipedia's human editors rather than replace them.

  • "I don't think you will ever see AI writing or generating Wikipedia articles," she said.
  • Asked whether she believes Wikipedia articles five years from now will still be written by humans for humans, Meehan replied: "I do."

Zoom out: Meehan also pointed out who and what gets left out if commercially developed AI becomes a principal gateway to knowledge.

  • Wikipedia exists in roughly 300 languages, including many that aren't likely to represent commercially attractive markets for AI companies.
  • She also raises the possibility of a knowledge divide in which the best access to information increasingly requires paying for an AI subscription.

The bottom line: Wikipedia spent the first phase of the generative AI boom becoming indispensable to AI. Its next challenge is ensuring that AI doesn't weaken the human and financial ecosystem that made Wikipedia indispensable in the first place.

item.title: Scoop: U.S. sent more Patriots to protect Saudi, Qatari energy sites
item.description:
The U.S. military in recent weeks sent two additional Patriot missile batteries to protect oil and gas facilities in Saudi Arabia and Qatar, two U.S. officials and one regional source said.

Why it matters: The U.S. wanted to reassure both allies that it would protect their key energy facilities in case President Trump decides to resume major combat operations against Iran.

  • Trump said on Thursday that he's considering renewing a bombing campaign in the coming weeks. "Now I have to make a decision: either Iran signs the deal, or it won't exist any longer," he said.

Flashback: In early August, when Trump was considering launching a massive attack that included strikes on Iranian energy infrastructure, the leaders of both Saudi Arabia and Qatar lobbied him not to do it. They expressed grave concern that Iran would strike their oil and natural gas facilities in retaliation.

  • U.S. officials said the pleas were a key reason Trump decided not to attack and move instead toward an economic pressure campaign.

Behind the scenes: Last month, the U.S. military sent one additional Patriot battery to Saudi Arabia to protect a key oil facility. Another Patriot battery was sent to Qatar to protect a natural gas facility.

  • The U.S. will need Saudi Arabia to allow it to use the country's airspace if major combat operations resume. But the Saudis are unlikely to grant permission if they feel oil facilities won't be protected.
  • A spokesman for U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM), Capt. Tim Hawkins, declined to comment.

Reality check: Patriot batteries and especially their interceptors have become a highly sought-after commodity since the war in Iran started.

  • The U.S. military transferred batteries and interceptors to the Middle East from other regional commands, raising concerns about readiness in other parts of the world.

State of play: The U.S. military is sending more warships, fighter jets and troops to the Middle East ahead of a possible resumption of the war.

  • A U.S. official said the USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier and its strike group left San Diego "quietly" on Sunday heading to the region. It's expected to arrive in the Middle East around mid-November.
  • The Roosevelt will join the USS George H.W. Bush, which has been in the region since March, and the USS George Washington, which was sent from Japan during the summer and has been in the region for only about a month.
  • "This means the Middle East region could potentially have up to three aircraft carrier strike groups. This is much more firepower," the U.S. official said.
  • But another U.S. official said it hasn't been determined whether the Roosevelt will replace one of the aircraft carriers currently deployed to the Middle East or whether it will be additional.

Zoom in: The Makin Island Amphibious Ready Group, which includes three amphibious ships carrying thousands of Marines from the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit, left for the region on Monday, a U.S. official said.

  • It is expected to arrive in the Middle East by the end of November and join another Amphibious Group and Marine expeditionary unit that have been deployed to the region over the last few months.

item.title: House Democrats' behind-the-scenes pitch for dues: Help us take on MAGA Inc.
item.description:
House Democratic leadership is pointing to the colossal spending by President Trump's super PACs in their behind-the-scenes efforts to get members to pay their dues to the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, Axios has learned.

Why it matters: DCCC dues have fueled heated infighting among House Democrats in recent months, with several proposals emerging to force members to cough up more money.

  • Some House Democrats want to require colleagues to pay their dues before seeking committee leadership roles, as The Washington Sun first reported.
  • But other lawmakers, particularly in the Progressive and Black Caucuses, are "furious" about these suggestions, said a senior House Democrat, who told Axios that "members ... don't like threats."

Driving the news: "While our case to the American people is strong, our Frontliners and candidates face ugly daily attacks from the right as MAGA Inc. unloads its coffers," DCCC chair Suzan DelBene (D-Wash.) wrote in an email to House Democrats obtained by Axios.

  • "We need the resources to fight back and support our battleground colleagues and candidates in these final weeks," she added.
  • DelBene ended the email with a plea for dues payments: "I urge everyone to make a dues contribution today. Let's make sure we don't have any regrets on Election Day."

Between the lines: While several House Democrats noted to Axios that DelBene routinely urges members to pay their dues — in emails and at caucus meetings — some clocked a more urgent tone than usual.

  • One lawmaker described the email, which was sent out on Wednesday, as "slightly more aggressive about shaming people" about not paying their dues than past entreaties.

By the numbers: A pair of super PACs linked to MAGA Inc. have emerged as two of the top spenders on congressional races nationwide despite launching in September.

  • No Going Back PAC and Safety and Affordability PAC have respectively spent $50 million and $38 million on ads in House races, according to ad tracking firm AdImpact.
  • That makes them the fourth and fifth largest outside ad spenders in the country, after Democrats' House Majority PAC and Republicans' Congressional Leadership Fund and American Action Network.

The intrigue: DelBene's email included the final version of House Democrats' August dues report, a draft copy of which was first reported by The Sun.

  • The report shows significant progress from April, with leadership going from 28 members who have paid 100% or more of their dues to 66.
  • Still, the August report lists 100 House Democrats as having paid 25% or less of their dues, including 38 who have paid none at all — though about half are swing-district members exempt from dues payments.

  • Still, the August report lists 100 House Democrats as having paid 25% or less of their dues, including 38 who have paid none at all — though about half are swing-district members exempt from dues payments.

item.title: Scoop: Dems beef with party leaders over snubbed Black candidates
item.description:
Democratic House leaders are being pressured by their members over the lack of Black candidates receiving top-level party support in the final weeks of the 2026 midterms, Axios has learned.

Why it matters: With 33 days to go, Democrats are torn between triaging their resources and satisfying all corners of their party's diverse but fractious racial coalition.

Zoom in: Some Black lawmakers have taken their concerns to Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) and DCCC chair and Rep. Suzan DelBene (D-Wash.) about the lack of Black candidates on the DCCC's "Red to Blue" list, according to a senior aide to a House Democrat.

  • Congressional Black Caucus Chair Yvette Clarke (D-N.Y.) spoke personally with DelBene about the lack of Black candidates on Red to Blue, according to two sources familiar with the matter.

The intrigue: The dearth of Black representation was a hot topic of conversation among legislators at the Congressional Black Caucus' annual conference in D.C. in September, three people told Axios.

  • "Members were openly talking about it, and they were pissed," said one Democratic operative.
  • "Red to Blue" provides fundraising and staffing assistance to contenders in swing districts.

The intrigue: Their push comes as some legislators argue that Democrats should do more to support Black candidates in the wake of a recent Supreme Court ruling that could threaten Black representation in Congress.

  • Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.), a CBC member, told Axios that "with the CBC under attack through gerrymandering and voter suppression, it's essential that the party invest in Black candidates."
  • In particular, she urged the DCCC to help Justin Pearson, a Black candidate running in a long-shot bid for Tennessee's 9th House District.
  • "Justin Pearson is an exceptional candidate who has proven that coalition-building and community-centered campaigns can make strides — even with the odds stacked against him," she said. "He is exactly the type of candidate the DCCC should be investing in."

Yes, but: Other CBC members say the party must be hard-nosed about its spending in 2026's final stretch, and that Black candidates such as Pearson and Raymond Smith in North Carolina's 3rd District are simply in territory that is too favorable to Republicans to warrant a serious investment.

  • "Jeffries, CBC PAC, DCCC, etc. can absolutely not be poor fiduciaries and spend money on races that are not attainable," one House Democrat told Axios in a text.
  • Added this lawmaker: "We need to make sure, next cycle, that we do a better job of recruiting Black candidates ... in actual Red to Blue seats. Not seats we wish were Red2Blue."
  • Some Democrats acknowledge that Pearson and Smith are facing an uphill battle in red districts. However, they argue, the DCCC has other ambitious races on its "Red to Blue" list that Cook Political Report rates solidly Republican and likely Republican, respectively.

The big picture: Jeffries was asked at a press conference on Wednesday about the lack of Black candidates in the "Red to Blue" program.

  • Jeffries said it is "largely a result of, you know, the primary process — there were in fact not a lot of candidates who stepped forward in these competitive districts."
  • He also defended the DCCC's record of supporting frontline Black candidates, such as Reps. Emilia Sykes (D-Ohio) and Jahana Hayes (D-Conn.).
  • "When I came into Congress, I think there were 38 members of the Congressional Black Caucus. Right now, there are 62," he said. "That's because the DCCC has actually partnered with the Congressional Black Caucus political action committee to grow the number of members of the CBC in districts that are overwhelmingly white."

What they're saying: "The CBC is in lockstep with Leader Jeffries," said CBC PAC spokesperson Chris Taylor in a statement.

  • "At his direction, the DCCC has backed our shared commitment to recruiting and investing to elect Black candidates and reach Black voters with real investment. Together, we will deliver the Democratic majority and make Hakeem Jeffries Speaker."
  • "We have enjoyed a strong partnership with the CBC PAC," said DCCC executive director Julie Merz in a statement. It noted that the group "began investing in talking to and organizing Black voters in key districts earlier than ever this election cycle."

Between the lines: This is not the first time the DCCC has caught heat from House Democrats' internal factions this year for its strategic decision-making.

  • Members of the Congressional Hispanic and Progressive Caucuses raged at the House Democratic campaign arm in June for spending $135,000 against a CHC- and CPC-backed primary candidate.

What's next: The DCCC's "Red to Blue" slate is ever-evolving, and there have been rumblings in Democratic circles in recent weeks that some Black candidates may soon be added to the program.

  • Jeffries said Wednesday that there "emerging opportunities in places throughout the South that we're closely monitoring."
  • A source familiar with the DCCC's planning said it expects to expand the battlefield further.

item.title: Mortgage rates approach 3-year high as new applications plunge
item.description:
Mortgage rates spiked to their highest level in nearly three years, continuing their climb above the 7% threshold.

Why it matters: Housing sales were already slow due to a lack of inventory and elevated rates, creating a risk that the market could further its freeze.

Zoom in: The weekly average 30-year fixed mortgage rate was 7.28% as of Thursday, Freddie Mac reported.

  • That's up 0.94 points from a year ago, and up 0.25 points from last week.
  • Mortgage rates closely track 10-year Treasury yields, which have risen by over 1.25 percentage points since the start of the Iran war in February.

The impact: Mortgage applications are plunging.

  • The Mortgage Bankers Association reported Wednesday that applications during the week ended Sept. 25 fell 6% from a week earlier.

With rates at their highest point since November 2023, home buyers are beginning to turn to adjustable-rate mortgages.

  • ARMs made up 10.3% of mortgage applications in the most recent period, marking the highest point since October 2025, according to MBA.
  • "Affordability and borrower demand have weakened in recent weeks as the higher-rate environment continues to put pressure on both prospective homebuyers and homeowners looking to refinance," MBA CEO Bob Broeksmit said in a statement.

What we're watching: There are early signs that rising rates could put downward pressure on prices as sellers look to attract buyers.

  • "Softer market conditions and greater affordability pressures have contributed to increased pricing pressures across many of our markets," KB Home senior VP William Hollinger said last week on an earnings call, noting the home builder had "made pricing adjustments."

Reality check: Rates may not remain elevated for long.

  • "We expect the situation to improve next year, as energy prices drop back and the aggressive Fed tightening cycle which has been priced into money markets does not fully materialise, causing mortgage rates to retrace most of their recent increases," Capital Economics senior North America economist Thomas Ryan wrote Tuesday.
  • Capital Economics projected that 30-year fixed mortgage rates would average 6.25% by the end of 2027.

item.title: Lawyers: Pike getting "life-saving care" after failed execution
item.description:
Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike's attorneys said she was "in critical condition" and "receiving life-saving care" Thursday, a day after she survived an execution attempt during which the state administered two doses of the lethal injection drug.

  • A death penalty expert told the Associated Press that Pike's survival after receiving the execution drug was unprecedented.

The latest: State and federal elected officials are pressing for public accountability after the second failed execution this year. Gov. Bill Lee halted further executions for the rest of the year and ordered a independent review of the Pike execution attempt.

  • On Thursday morning, he told reporters there were "very few answers" about what had gone wrong.

U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, the frontrunner to succeed Lee as governor next year, blasted the "botched process" in a statement and pushed for the state to "bring back the electric chair."

Pike's attorneys told reporters Thursday that Lee's pledge to launch an investigation did not go far enough. They urged him to commute her death sentence.

What they're saying: Attorney Randy Spivey, who was inside the prison during the execution attempt, said prison officials spent about an hour trying to establish IV access. He counted at least seven needles used in Pike's left arm alone.

  • Pike complained of sharp pain during the lethal injection. Spivey said he noticed her right arm turning purple, especially after the second round of chemicals. He said the lawyers had also been told of blistering and burning around the injection sites.

Between the lines: Federal public defender Stephen Ferrell said the lawyers had warned courts months earlier about medical problems with Pike's veins that made it harder to establish an IV.

Zoom in: The attorneys also said they weren't able to quickly reach their colleagues or court officials responsible for overseeing the execution.

  • Spivey said it took seven minutes and passage through six locked doors to get to a telephone so he could reach the rest of Pike's legal team.
  • Ferrell said an emergency telephone number provided for the Tennessee Supreme Court went to voicemail.

The state's response: Lee called the latest failed execution "a tragedy" on Thursday morning.

  • "It's deeply disturbing to me that that has happened in this state," he told reporters, according to Reuters.

The big picture: This isn't the first time Tennessee's prison officials have faced scrutiny for their approach to the death penalty. After a 2022 execution was halted over failures to properly test the drugs, Lee paused all executions so the state could investigate and overhaul its lethal injection protocol.

  • Executions resumed last year.

But more problems surfaced in 2026. Tennessee prison officials abruptly stopped another inmate's execution in May after staff had difficulties finding a vein for an IV line used in the lethal injection.

  • Critics blasted prison officials for disregarding Pike's concerns that there might be similar problems during her execution.

Zoom out: Pike was convicted and sentenced to death for the 1995 beating death of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. Her legal team does not contest her guilt.

  • Slemmer's mother, May Martinez, traveled to Nashville this week to witness the execution.
  • "It was a mess," she told NBC News early Thursday. "They went to try to execute her, and she didn't die."

Martinez vented her anger with the governor and prison officials: "They f----- up."

item.title: Christa Pike's execution failed. Here's how lethal injection works
item.description:
Lethal injections are under scrutiny after Christa Pike survived two rounds of drugs during Tennessee's failed attempt to execute her.

Why it matters: Lethal injection has been the dominant U.S. execution method for decades, accounting for roughly 89% of the 1,683 executions carried out since 1976, per the Death Penalty Information Center.

Driving the news: Pike, convicted of killing a classmate three decades ago, survived two rounds of lethal injection drugs Wednesday in what would have been the state's first execution of a woman in 200 years.

  • In response, Gov. Bill Lee halted executions and ordered a "comprehensive, third-party review" of the failed attempt.
  • Pike's execution attempt followed hours of legal whiplash in which courts first stayed the execution before reversing course.
  • Pike is still alive as of Thursday afternoon, her attorney said at a news conference, according to the AP. She is receiving "lifesaving care" after a failed attempt Wednesday night that her attorney said amounted to "torture."

The big picture: Execution protocols vary by state, but lethal injections generally follow the same basic process.

Here's what to know.

Update: The map labels were changed to consolidate primary and secondary execution methods. Data: Death Penalty Information Center; Note: New Hampshire abolished the death penalty but retains one prisoner on death row; Map: Erin Davis/Axios

Why states adopted lethal injection

Flashback: Lethal injections emerged after the Supreme Court allowed capital punishment to return in the 1970s.

  • Oklahoma became the first state to authorize the practice in 1977. Texas carried out its first five years later.
  • Before lethal injections, states commonly used methods like electrocution, gas, hanging and firing squads. Lawmakers considered injections to be less violent and cheaper.

Lethal injections are now used in all death penalty states.

  • The Supreme Court requires states to reserve the death penalty only for the most heinous murders.

Several states — Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah — allow firing squads.

  • Idaho made firing squad its primary execution method in July.

How lethal injections are administered

There isn't one standard procedure. States use different protocols, but the basic process is similar.

  • A fatal dose of drugs is delivered through an IV while the prisoner is restrained, often to a gurney.
  • Arizona, for example, requires two IV catheters, one as a backup in case the first line fails.

Physicians often don't administer lethal injections because the American Medical Association's Code of Medical Ethics says doctors should not participate in executions.

  • States instead sometimes rely on execution teams that can include prison guards, corrections employees and other personnel trained to administer the drugs.

What drugs are used in lethal injections

How it works: There are two main ways these drugs are administered.

  • One drug path — The state administers a sedative or barbiturate, commonly pentobarbital, to cause death.
  • Three drug path — Another method includes giving a sedative or anesthetic, then a paralytic before a final drug stops the heart.

Yes, but: Pentobarbital itself is controversial, with critics questioning whether it really causes a painless death.

  • A Justice Department review under the Biden administration cited concerns that the drug possibly caused pain and suffering.
  • President Trump's DOJ reauthorized the federal use of pentobarbital.

Lethal injections don't always work as planned

Pike's case is not the first lethal injection gone wrong. The DPIC says 75 of 1,054 lethal injections (about 7%) were botched from 1890 to 2010 — the most of any method.

What they're saying: Witnesses to some executions have described prisoners gasping for air and struggling to breathe.

  • Some prisoners survive the initial attempt but later die from complications or other medical causes, sometimes linked to the execution attempt. Others are executed at a later date.
  • Autopsies have found evidence of prisoner suffering from pulmonary edema, which is a buildup of fluid in the lungs that can create the same sensation as drowning, per NPR.

Case in point: In 2022, Alabama called off Kenneth Smith's execution after officials couldn't insert an IV before his death warrant expired.

  • Smith survived but was later executed in 2024 through nitrogen hypoxia, a first in American history.
  • In 2014, the execution of Clayton Lockett in Oklahoma went badly after officials failed to properly establish an IV. He died nearly an hour later.

Go deeper: America is seeing an uptick in executions

item.title: Netanyahu: Omani co-pilot went through Islamic radicalization
item.description:
The initial investigation into the attempted hijacking of the FlyDubai flight from the UAE to Israel found that the co-pilot went through religious Islamic radicalization in recent months, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told Fox News Thursday.

Why it matters: Netanyahu's remarks, confirmed by an Israeli intelligence official and people who worked with the co-pilot, strengthen the possibility that the incident was a terrorist attack.

Driving the news: The investigation is being led by the Saudi security services, which have been interrogating the co-pilot who allegedly attacked the other pilot while the plane was en route from Dubai to Tel Aviv.

  • The United Arab Emirates has formed a team to investigate the incident. "The investigation includes examining all circumstances and motives surrounding the incident, including any possible connection to terrorist activity or intent, and whether it involved prior planning or direction," a spokeswoman for Emirati Foreign Minister Afra Alhameli said in a statement.

Behind the scenes: An Israeli intelligence official said the Mossad and Shin Bet spy agencies are also investigating.

  • "The Omani co-pilot went through a process of religious radicalization in recent years. We don't know yet if he is a 'lone wolf' or whether he was sent by someone to conduct an attack," the official said.

The intrigue: On Wednesday, Israel's Channel 16 reported testimony of another FlyDubai pilot who knew the Omani co-pilot.

  • According to the report, the co-pilot worked for the company for only eight months and was more religiously observant than most of his co-workers.

What he's saying: President Trump told reporters Thursday he has reason to believe Iran was involved in the foiled hijacking. "Based on what I'm hearing is yes, but we're working on it right now," he said.

  • Israeli officials say they currently don't have indications of Iranian involvement, by they haven't ruled it out.
  • The Saudi Ministry of Interior said in a statement that UAE officials took part in the interrogation of the pilot and co-pilot. Both have been transferred to the UAE for further interrogation, per the statement.

What to watch: One of the things that will be investigated is how an Omani national was assigned as a pilot on a flight to Israel.

  • According to security protocols agreed to by the UAE and Israel, crew members from countries that don't have diplomatic relations with Israel can't serve on flights to Israel.

The intrigue: On Wednesday, Israel's Channel 16 reported testimony of another FlyDubai pilot who knew the Omani co-pilot.

  • According to the report, the co-pilot worked for the company for only eight months and was more religiously observant than most of his co-workers.

What he's saying: President Trump told reporters Thursday he has reason to believe Iran was involved in the foiled hijacking. "Based on what I'm hearing is yes, but we're working on it right now," he said.

  • Israeli officials say they currently don't have indications of Iranian involvement, by they haven't ruled it out.
  • The Saudi Ministry of Interior said in a statement that UAE officials took part in the interrogation of the pilot and co-pilot. Both have been transferred to the UAE for further interrogation, per the statement.

What to watch: One of the things that will be investigated is how an Omani national was assigned as a pilot on a flight to Israel.

  • According to security protocols agreed to by the UAE and Israel, crew members from countries that don't have diplomatic relations with Israel can't serve on flights to Israel.

item.title: British Iranian arrested in U.K. terror plot probe
item.description:
A U.K. Iranian dual national was arrested on suspicion of preparing to carry out terrorist acts in connection with an incident at an English air base used by the U.S., British counterterrorism police said Thursday.

The big picture: Tehran has denied any involvement in the suspected bomb plot at RAF Fairford, while U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were "strong indications that Iran played a part" in it.

Driving the news: The 27-year-old man was arrested in Westminster, London, on Thursday afternoon on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts under Section 5 of the Terrorism Act 2006, per a Counter Terrorism Policing statement.

  • Police also questioned a 26-year-old British man and searched two properties in the area.
  • Five men in their 20s, who were arrested on Sunday following the early morning incident remain on police bail, according to the statement.

Context: The British government earlier this year allowed the U.S. to use RAF Fairford for limited defensive strikes against Iranian missile capabilities.

  • Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps noted in July that U.S. B-1 bombers flew from RAF Fairford and said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory is a legitimate target for us."

State of play: Senior National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing Vicki Evans in a statement described the investigation into circumstances surrounding the incident in Gloucestershire as "hugely complex."

  • Specialist teams are "interrogating multiple lines of enquiry," she said.
  • "As we've made clear, we're looking at all possible angles – including possible foreign state involvement."

item.title: The Fed's long-term interest rate problem
item.description:
The relentless rise in long-term interest rates is starting to have effects on more parts of the economy, Kansas City Fed president Jeff Schmid told Axios Thursday.

  • "You're starting to see some friction in some of the long-market users of credit," he said, pointing to multifamily housing and commercial lending.
  • "Even on the mortgage rate side, it's starting to affect home prices, which is how the price of credit works relative to valuation," Schmid said at a conference on investing in rural America hosted by the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond in Asheville, N.C.

The big picture: Schmid spoke alongside Richmond Fed president Tom Barkin and Boston Fed president Susan Collins, who weighed in on the forces driving the rise in borrowing costs.

  • "I think you're seeing this trillion-dollar AI buildout, and I think it's not surprising that rates go up if you've got a lot more demand out there," Barkin added.

Collins said AI investment is also helping drive the solid economic growth that has persisted despite higher borrowing costs.

  • "I think it does have broader effects, not just in particular sectors," Collins said. But it "remains to be seen" whether investment will continue at its current pace, she added.

The intrigue: Schmid likened the Fed's challenge of separating strong demand from supply-driven inflation to a seven-layer dip — one of his favorite foods.

  • "The beauty of a seven-layer dip is you have equal amounts of beans and sour cream," Schmid said. Right now, with AI and data centers, "there's too much beans in that dip," he added.
  • "And not enough chips!" quipped Barkin.

item.title: World opinion shifts on trade
item.description:
More countries are buying into a core piece of President Trump's argument about what is broken in global trade, even as his tariffs rattle the world economy.

Why it matters: Two major agreements over the past month show that more countries are embracing the view that huge trade imbalances and excess production can hurt domestic industries and may warrant action.

Driving the news: G20 trade officials are in Milwaukee this week, where they announced a new agreement to tackle the global steel glut.

  • The "Milwaukee Framework" calls on countries to curb market-distorting subsidies and step up monitoring of steel imports and trade circumvention.
  • It also endorses "evidence-based actions" against excess capacity, including possibly tariffs.

That agreement follows a broader acknowledgment at the G20 finance ministers meeting in Asheville, N.C., in September.

  • The U.S. and nearly every other G20 economy there agreed that large, persistent trade imbalances can harm other countries. They signed on to a statement that asked nations with big surpluses to address policies that leave them overly reliant on exports for growth.
  • China was the lone G20 member present to object to that statement.

Between the lines: For decades, governments have warned about distortions in global trade, including excess steel production. What is changing: the willingness to acknowledge the damage to domestic industries and protect them.

  • "Most countries agree with these global issues, people agree with the diagnosis, but they're loath to action," U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told reporters on the sidelines of the conference. He said the Milwaukee agreement "couldn't have happened in 2015."
  • "All these other countries — they know that if they want to continue to have access to the U.S. market, we need to adjust the international system," Greer said. "As we come with creative ideas and new structures and cohesive plans, they're coming on board."

Zoom out: EU trade chief Maroš Šefčovič welcomed the administration's focus on excess capacity at a roundtable with Greer and manufacturing CEOs at Rockwell Automation's Milwaukee headquarters on Tuesday.

  • European industries are being crushed by cheap imports driven by global overcapacity, much of it from China. Europe is responding with more trade barriers of its own — possibly including harsher tariffs.
  • "I think a lot of folks in Europe, including the trade commissioner and others, I think they're pretty clear-eyed about this issue…. They're starting to go through some of the steps we started going through 10 years ago," Greer said, adding he believes Europe itself contribute to global excess capacity.

The other side: U.S. trading partners are dealing with tariffs, or the prospect of tariffs, aimed at some of the same problems they are working with Washington to address.

  • Most Canadian steel exports to the U.S. face a 50% tariff. An import ban on certain Canadian products took effect as one of the nation's trade officials arrived in Milwaukee.
  • Greer is also investigating excess capacity and production in 16 economies — probes that could ultimately clear the way for fresh tariffs.
  • Greer acknowledged that tension at the roundtable, noting that the U.S. and its trading partners may have disputes with one another but still share concerns about excess production elsewhere.

The intrigue: Foreign trade ministers piled into coach buses yesterday afternoon for a 1.5-mile trip to Rockwell Automation's Milwaukee headquarters, where they toured the factory floor.

  • The "field trip" was intended to show the kind of advanced domestic manufacturing the Trump administration wants to encourage.
  • Rockwell gave the ministers steel-toed sneakers for the tour (which were made in Vietnam).

Zoom in: Rockwell, which makes automation technology used on factory floors, is investing $2 billion in U.S. plants, talent and technology. But tariffs are also raising costs for the manufacturer.

  • Rockwell told investors over the summer that some of its customers are delaying projects.
  • "In such a volatile environment with respect to tariffs and inflation, they want to make sure that the cost side of their business case is solid," CEO Blake Moret said on the company's earnings call.

The bottom line: Trump-era tariffs are divisive, but the president's case for rethinking the global trading system is proving less so.

item.title: 5 takeaways from Trump's combative Time interview
item.description:
President Trump's 75-minute interview with Time revealed his latest thinking on the Iran war, the AI race (or in his words, SI), the media and more.

Why it matters: The interview with one of America's most historic news publications gives voters insight into the direction of the country roughly a month ahead of the midterms.

Driving the news: Trump was unapologetic across the board: on prolonging the Iran war, resisting AI regulation and threatening to "go after" Democrats if they win the House.

  • The interview was historic, too, as it was Trump's 56th appearance on a Time cover, "surpassing President Richard Nixon, who held the record for more than half a century," the magazine says.

Here are five takeaways.

Trump on Iran:

Trump was defiant when asked why the war in Iran had stretched longer than the timeline he originally floated, telling Time, "I could have stopped then, but I wanted to go further."

  • He said the press "fed" Americans his initial prediction of attacks lasting around four to six weeks, a timeline he gave to multiple outlets at the start of the war. He also repeatedly suggested the war was almost over.

He reiterated the threat he made before the UN General Assembly that he may "annihilate" Iran.

  • Pressed to square that with the assertion that he's the president of peace, Trump replied, "by annihilating Iran, we've created peace in the world."
  • He also said it's "possible" he'd ramp up bombing after the midterms, disputing Pentagon reports of a munitions shortfall.

Trump on Netanyahu reelection:

Trump sidestepped questions about whether Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu should be reelected in Israel, with the election just weeks away.

  • He said he was "not involved in politics anymore" but touted his popularity in Israel.
  • Pressed again, Trump applauded U.S. support for Israel, saying, "No, my primary thing—I do want to help them defend Israel."

On Netanyahu's leading opposition candidate and former Israel Defense Forces chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, Trump said, "I don't hear bad things about him."

  • But he added, "people have written off Bibi [Netanyahu] many, many times, just like they've written off me many, many times. I wouldn't underestimate Bibi."
President Trump meets with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the Oval Office on July 28. Photo: Ma'ayan Toaf/GPO/Handout/Anadolu via Getty Images

Trump on the AI race and superintelligence:

Trump continued to brush aside concerns about AI's threat to humanity as "phony threats."

  • Asked by Time who's behind that conspiracy, Trump replied, "The whole country is based on fake stuff because these people have Trump derangement syndrome."

He said he didn't know if that included Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who dined with the president on Sunday.

  • The president said his "guardrail" if top AI labs "do bad things" is federal law enforcement: "I have a DOJ, I have an FBI."

Trump also championed the data centers powering the AI boom, despite widespread opposition.

  • "I would like to have data centers," he said. "It doesn't mean I want them right next to my house, but certainly I like them in my county."
  • He acknowledged "so many politicians are against them," but warned, "If we don't build them, they'll be built someplace else."
A screenshot of a White House post about the Time magazine cover. Screenshot: @WhiteHouse/X

Trump pressed on the media ban, coverage:

After banning three media outlets from the White House — and being ordered by a judge to reinstate them, Trump continued to blast "fake news" for what he called "bad story after bad story."

  • It comes as the White House once again dropped CNN from the press pool covering the president's trip to Texas and Oklahoma Thursday.

He also lashed out at Time for the questions they asked him, saying in response to an inquiry about Sen. Mitch McConnell's (R-Ky.) health, "You haven't asked me one f--king positive question."

  • He ended the interview by saying, "Well, I hope I get a decent story. I don't think—you know, it's hard to get a good story. Every question's a hit. I don't know what the hell's wrong."

How Trump views Democrats

Trump told Time that he doesn't think Democrats will take control of Congress after the midterms — especially if he campaigns.

  • "I think we'll do okay if I campaign, and I intend to. If I campaign … you don't give me enough credit. When I campaign, I give people a lot."

If Democrats win the House, Trump predicted: "They'll probably go after me and I'll go after them."

  • There was at least one Democrat Trump was willing to praise: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. "I say I like him, I think he's great, but I think his policies are crazy."

Go deeper: How Trump's signature issue fell off voters' radar

item.title: The rocky road to a new permitting law
item.description:
A sweeping bipartisan deal to cut permitting red tape faces a long road ahead despite a broad show of support.

Why it matters: Cutting hurdles for energy projects is a top priority for fossil fuels and renewables sectors, but some green groups fear erosion of safeguards.

  • Powerful business groups want to make building all sorts of infrastructure easier.

Driving the news: Top Republicans and Democrats on the Senate's energy and environment panels on Wednesday dropped the 417-page bill that includes:

  • New limits on the duration of lawsuits, and the scope and length of reviews under the Clean Water Act and National Environmental Policy Act.
  • A stronger federal hand in siting and approval of large transmission projects.
  • Protections for previously issued permits, a priority for renewables groups and Dems upset with Trump administration barriers.

The big picture: A who's who of major business and energy industry groups — representing oil and gas, renewables and coal — cheered the bill.

  • The White House backs the deal and wants quick passage, an official said.

State of play: The deal still has a long road ahead. Co-author Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) said Wednesday at a press conference that there will be revisions as backers seek input from colleagues.

  • There are also "unresolved" questions about Trump officials returning to "regular order" for wind and solar projects, Whitehouse said.
  • But he credited the administration with a "very reasonable opening proposal" on the matter.
  • Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), the top Democrat on the Natural Resources Committee, criticized the bill and said his party will have a stronger hand next year.

Center-left backers see a huge opening to help build out clean energy and grid upgrades to integrate it.

  • But groups on the left flank of the climate movement panned it, calling it a giveaway to fossil fuel interests.

What we're watching: Some groups with close ties to Democrats staked out a noncommittal-to-positive position, saying they need more time to study the bill.

  • The Natural Resources Defense Council cheered transmission pieces while saying it's unclear if they outweigh "rollbacks" of environmental laws, and said it "must improve."
  • Evergreen Action welcomed project certainty and transmission sections but added that changes to key environmental laws demand "diligent scrutiny."

Zoom in: The bill would prevent utility ratepayers from bearing the costs of new power and grid upgrades needed for AI data centers.

  • Everyone's still digesting the intricate bill, but in principle, turning this bipartisan goal into firm requirements could ease political hurdles.

The bottom line: Two things are true — the odds of a big permitting deal are at their highest in a very long time, and many things could trip this up.

Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

  • But groups on the left flank of the climate movement panned it, calling it a giveaway to fossil fuel interests.

What we're watching: Some groups with close ties to Democrats staked out a noncommittal-to-positive position, saying they need more time to study the bill.

  • The Natural Resources Defense Council cheered transmission pieces while saying it's unclear if they outweigh "rollbacks" of environmental laws, and said it "must improve."
  • Evergreen Action welcomed project certainty and transmission sections but added that changes to key environmental laws demand "diligent scrutiny."

Zoom in: The bill would prevent utility ratepayers from bearing the costs of new power and grid upgrades needed for AI data centers.

  • Everyone's still digesting the intricate bill, but in principle, turning this bipartisan goal into firm requirements could ease political hurdles.

The bottom line: Two things are true — the odds of a big permitting deal are at their highest in a very long time, and many things could trip this up.

item.title: Trump, Big AI go all-in together
item.description:
President Trump and the AI industry have co-signed one of the biggest economic and technological wagers of all time.

  • If it goes right: A new age of abundance — explosive productivity, staggering wealth and a generational leap in American power.
  • If it goes wrong: A catastrophic bust that destroys capital and jobs and, in the words of several involved, threatens widespread human harm.

Why it matters: Neither Trump nor the AI titans have plausible deniability. Their fortunes have become so tightly bound that success will be shared — and failure impossible to disown.

The big picture: Trump and Big AI have fused their futures around four enormous bets.

1. The economic bet: That trillions poured into chips, data centers and power will create a productivity engine powerful enough to fuel a new Industrial Revolution.

  • AI infrastructure spending is projected to reach $10.3 trillion by 2032, but the payoff remains unproven: One analysis found hyperscalers have spent nearly $1 trillion more on AI since 2024 than AI has generated in revenue.
  • The promise sold by Trump and his tech allies is a new era of growth and abundance. The peril is a historic misallocation of capital on a scale few industries have ever seen.

2. The regulation bet: That Washington can clear the runway for an AI takeoff while leaving the companies largely responsible for policing themselves.

  • The new White House accord signed by Trump and the AI giants enshrines voluntary safeguards, company-led testing and third-party reviews instead of new federal mandates.
  • The promise is American dominance over China. The peril is that self-regulation fails, forcing Washington to intervene only after damage has already been inflicted.

3. The safety bet: That AI can grow vastly more powerful without becoming vastly harder to control.

  • Many of the most dire safety warnings come from AI researchers themselves. Anthropic's own IPO prospectus contemplates scenarios in which advanced AI kills humanity.
  • The promise is almost limitless: superintelligent systems that help cure diseases and accelerate scientific discovery. The peril is self-improving AI that evolves faster than its creators can comprehend or contain.

4. The political bet: That Trump and Big AI can become inseparable without making each other even more toxic.

  • Trump has staked his legacy on winning the AI race — dismissing fears about data centers costing Republicans in the midterms — while the industry has staked billions on the policy environment he's creating.
  • The promise is that Trump and Big AI become partners in the defining technological transformation of the century. The peril is that every AI failure, disruption or backlash becomes a liability they share.

The bottom line: Trump and the AI industry are asking the country for a leap of faith at a uniquely fragile moment for both.

  • Americans are deeply dissatisfied with both the economy and Trump's presidency, with his approval rating plunging to record lows ahead of a potentially disastrous midterm season.
  • The AI industry faces an even more basic credibility problem: A new Quinnipiac poll found 74% of Americans lack trust in AI executives, while only 34% believe AI will do more good than harm in their daily lives.

item.title: Trump and CEOs try to shed AI's toxic branding
item.description:
The great AI rebranding is on, led by President Trump and tech titans like Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who are embracing an alternative term: "super intelligence," or SI.

Why it matters: Leaders in D.C. and Silicon Valley are worried the public backlash against AI and data centers will hamper the development of this staggeringly powerful and existentially dangerous technology. The new label is part of a broader effort to shift the narrative.

Driving the news: Flanked by the most powerful figures in tech on Tuesday, Trump officially declared "super intelligence" the preferred terminology of the executive branch. He'd previously solicited alternative terms for AI on Truth Social.

  • "Now we're calling it, again, super. We can say the word super, because the other word is a fake word," Trump said after Tuesday's White House summit. Leaders from Google, Anthropic, Meta, OpenAI, xAI and Nvidia all signed the "White House Accord on Super Intelligence."
  • Huang has recently extended the label to physical infrastructure, referring to data centers as "super intelligence factories." Opposition to the huge, energy-guzzling facilities is dimming the prospects for fast-growing AI firms and some congressional candidates.

Between the lines: A rose by any other name would smell as sweet, and AI by any other name will likely seem as scary.

  • Communities are building bipartisan coalitions against data centers, younger workers are anxious about their career prospects, and AI insiders continue to warn about catastrophic risks, notes Axios Communicators author Simon Hernandez-Arthur.
  • Calling it "super intelligence" attempts to evoke the technology's promise without immediately bringing to mind all that negative baggage.

What they're saying: Some of the tech executives who appeared with Trump continued to use "AI" in their remarks, but xAI CEO Elon Musk caught himself and pivoted to "SI." Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has long used "superintelligence" branding.

  • Huang, CEO of the world's most valuable company, appears to be leading the charge. He used the term twice in a post and repeatedly invoked it in a panel discussion at the White House. When he slipped once and said "AI," Huang corrected himself: "I am going to get good at this."
  • AI company representatives declined to comment about the name change on the record. Some said their companies were generally supportive of the rebrand and plan to use "SI" when meeting with the president and working with the federal government. Others said they didn't expect it to catch fire outside of those contexts.
  • One source compared it to Trump's renaming of the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America, which many (though not all) oil executives adopted in their external and internal communications.

By the numbers: "SI" has yet to catch on with the public. A YouGov poll conducted this week found that 53% of respondents considered "artificial intelligence" the better term for the tech, vs. 9% who preferred "super intelligence."

The bottom line: Trump said on Tuesday that "artificial" intelligence made the technology sound like a hoax: "The name is now super intelligence. That's not a hoax, in fact it's the exact opposite."

  • Polls suggest most Americans agree with him that AI is anything but a hoax. That's why they're so worried.

item.title: How Trump's signature issue fell off voters' radar
item.description:
Immigration — the issue that helped propel Donald Trump to the presidency and rally his supporters over the past decade — has become an afterthought for voters.

Why it matters: It's another ominous sign for Trump and the GOP heading toward November. What was once a rallying cry for the party is losing salience with voters across the spectrum — and harsh crackdowns have even made it a liability among some Republicans.

  • "On net, Republicans win out as the more trusted party on only two topics, and it's border/immigration [and] crime and safety," said Avery James of Echelon Insights, a Republican polling firm. "But the problem if you're a campaign strategist is quite simple: crime and immigration are just not the top issues for voters."

The big picture: Just two years ago, immigration was a top concern for voters nationwide, especially self-identified Republicans.

  • After President Biden dropped his reelection bid, the GOP spent half its advertising budget on immigration-related ads, per an AdImpact analysis.
  • "If you ask [about] immigration as an overall issue that people care about, it went from like a top three issue two years ago to way down the list now, in single digits," said Erik Iverson, a GOP pollster working with the Republican Senate campaign arm.

Between the lines: Pollsters say concern about immigration peaked during Biden's tenure, when illegal border crossings and asylum seekers at the Southern border surged.

  • But weeks into Trump's term, crossings dropped dramatically after he deployed the U.S. military at the border, instituted a ban on asylum claims and paused refugee admissions.
  • "You become a victim of your own success," Iverson said.

Zoom in: Cost of living ranks as the top issue for voters, far outpacing immigration. That's especially bad news for Republicans trying to turn out voters in competitive statewide races.

  • More than half of Texas Republicans and one-quarter of independents said border security and immigration was Texas's most important problem about one year ago, according University of Texas poll. Its latest survey, conducted in August, shows that figure cut in half.
  • In Michigan, only 14% of all voters said it was their top issue in a survey for AARP co-conducted by Trump pollster Fabrizio Ward.
  • A September poll of Ohio voters shows a higher share concerned about immigration, 25%, when asked to name their top three issues. But it was dwarfed by a combined 70% who were most concerned about the economy and inflation.
  • "That issue just dropped with Republicans because they weren't seeing it every day. They weren't feeling threatened by it every day," said Brent Buchanan, of Cygnal, a Republican polling firm.

The intrigue: Tying immigration to the economy and cost of living still resonates with low-propensity Trump voters, according to polling Iverson recently shared with Senate Republicans.

  • And Buchanan said that border security can still be used effectively to draw a contrast between candidates in specific races. But it's unlikely to drive turnout among what he called "soft Republicans."

By the numbers: Voters are starting to sour on Trump's handling of immigration.

  • His disapproval rating on immigration jumped to 58% in a late August survey from Ipsos, up from 38% when Trump took office last year.

Stunning stat: A September New York Times/Siena poll showed Democrats are more trusted on immigration than Republicans by 51 to 45%. Most other polling, however, still shows Republicans ahead on the issue.

  • "Everyone likes enforcement until it hits close to home or they get the wrong person. It's not necessarily the policies. It's the tactics that are turning people off. There has to be a middle ground," a former White House official said.

The other side: "Americans are less concerned about immigration because President Trump stopped the invasion of our country and delivered the most secure border in American history," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement. "Thanks to President Trump's strong immigration enforcement policies, approximately three million illegals have left the United States and zero illegals have been released at the border in sixteen months."

What they're saying: The polling trends are giving Democrats a new opening, especially in areas with sizable Hispanic populations.

  • Republicans are "trying so hard to distance themselves from Trump on the overall immigration issue because they know it is toxic with Latino voters right now," said Stephanie Valencia, founder of the Latino-focused polling firm Equis.
  • "Democrats should be giving Trump credit for the control and the maintenance of the U.S.-Mexico border," she said. But "at the end of the day, people are asking for a lot more than that."

item.title: GOP senators endure painful week with little to show for it
item.description:
Exhausted GOP senators are preparing to fly home mostly empty-handed after staying in D.C. longer than expected.

Why it matters: The midterm outlook is getting bleaker by the day, and Republicans have a monster to-do list for the lame-duck session that could be a last chance to capitalize on their trifecta.

Between the lines: Republicans decided against breaking for an early recess last week.

  • The biggest thing to show for it: A historic — and bipartisan — college sports package that doesn't do much for those defending their seats in November. It faces long odds in the House.

😖 Otherwise it was a week of pain:

  • Failed votes: A vote addressing Americans' concerns about data centers driving up energy costs failed today, as did another to curb congressional stock trades and enforce voter IDs.
  • A line of attack that backfired: A major hearing with Jack Smith was overshadowed by a failed attempt by Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.) to link the special counsel and Atlanta prosecutor Fani Willis.
  • The Trump issue: Republicans have been tiptoeing around whether Trump's unpopularity will hurt the party in November, only for Texas nominee Ken Paxton to be caught blaming Trump's midterm convention for hurting his polling.
  • NRSC Chair Tim Scott (R-S.C.) said Paxton's analysis was "just wrong" and called the convention "a boost in the right direction."

🤕 Zoom out: Some of the GOP senators are returning to fresh campaign headaches.

  • Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) lost a week of in-state campaigning and didn't even get a vote on one of her key priorities: a bipartisan bill to lower insulin costs.
  • Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.) is the target of a new ad campaign hitting him over his pardon of a man who pleaded guilty to first-degree sexual assault.
  • Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) has been batting down accusations that he went after mothers of new babies over unpaid medical bills. His lawyers sent a cease-and-desist letter to his opponent — Rev. Adam Hamilton — on Monday.

The GOP has a cash advantage, but the campaign apparatus now has to spend heavily in states Trump handily won in 2024 — Ohio, Iowa, Alaska, Texas, Kansas, Nebraska and Florida.

‼️ The other side: Former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) was also hit with a damaging report from the New York Times about her personal behavior and office culture (some of which she denied). She is challenging GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan.

What to watch: The Senate will return in November staring down a list of must-pass items.

  • Fund the government
  • Pass the National Defense Authorization Act
  • Reinstate FISA Section 702, the warrantless wiretap authority
  • Pass the farm bill

💰 The bottom line: That's just what they must get done. There's also a growing list of maybe-to-dos, like:

  • Take a whack at a bipartisan permitting reform bill that finally came together hours before the Senate took off for home.
  • Pass some form of AI guardrails.
  • Raise the debt ceiling, potentially through reconciliation.

item.title: Scoop: Rubio ordered Iranian delegation to leave the country, U.S. official says
item.description:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio demanded on Monday that the Iranian delegation to the United Nations General Assembly immediately leave the country after negotiations stalled, according to a U.S. official and a second source with knowledge of the matter.

Why it matters: Though the Iranians were likely to depart soon anyway, Rubio's move was a highly unusual diplomatic rebuke and laid bare the deep distrust between the two countries amid fruitless efforts to broker an end to the war.

  • Qatari mediators tried to secure a diplomatic breakthrough between the U.S. and Iran but made little progress, with neither side willing to budge.
  • Among those ordered to leave New York was Rubio's Iranian counterpart, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.

What they're saying: "Secretary Rubio kicked out the Iranian delegation who had overstayed their welcome. The UN General Assembly was over, so it was time for them to go," the U.S. official said.

Behind the scenes: On Monday morning, the White House thought there might be progress in talks with Iran later in the day. But by late afternoon it became clear negotiations were at a stalemate.

  • Then on Monday evening, at Rubio's orders, the U.S. mission to the UN told the Iranian mission to the UN that Araghchi's delegation had to leave New York immediately, according to the U.S. official.
  • The Iranian delegation, including Araghchi, left for the airport several hours later and boarded a flight from New York to Doha at 1:20 a.m. Tuesday.
  • A second source confirmed that the U.S. demanded that the Iranian delegation leave, but said Araghchi was scheduled to travel back to Tehran on Monday night anyway.

What's next: Qatari mediators are continuing to talk to both sides about their compromise proposal, regional sources say.

  • "Maybe I will blow 'em up," President Trump told reporters on Wednesday when asked how he can reach a deal with a regime he says is crazy. "Maybe I blow 'em up. We have to make that decision. We will blow 'em up or make a deal. But the time is coming. It's gonna end very soon one way or the other."

item.title: Netanyahu says FlyDubai pilots prevented a "9/11 disaster"
item.description:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu revealed new details about a FlyDubai flight bound for Israel during which a pilot stabbed a colleague, sending the plane spiraling thousands of feet.

The big picture: Netanyahu told CNN Wednesday evening that the Indian pilot who was stabbed, Capt. Smit Machchhar, unlocked the cockpit after being attacked and an Israeli passenger who works as a plumber, Yaniv Hayun, entered and found the Omani pilot apparently trying to interfere with the aircraft's controls.

  • Netanyahu said the suspect was being interrogated in Saudi Arabia and that the UAE agreed Israel could participate in the interrogation.

What they're saying: The Israeli prime minister told CNN's Jim Sciutto that passengers heard shouts and screams coming from the cockpit and that the plumber saw the attacking pilot hovering over the instruments, noting "he was trying to jam the instruments."

  • The plumber pulled back on the aircraft's controls, while another passenger and crew member subdued the attacker, according to Netanyahu. Reserve pilots then came in and stabilized the plane.
  • Netanyahu said he met Hayun at the airport and that the passenger was "drenched" in the Indian pilot's blood.

President Trump said Netanyahu and others had briefed him on what happened.

  • He called the stabbed pilot a "hero" for managing to open the cockpit door and also praised the plumber's actions.

Flashback: Netanyahu noted his own history with hijackings: He was wounded while taking part in the 1972 Israeli commando raid that freed passengers from a hijacked Sabena flight. His brother Yoni was killed four years later while leading the Entebbe hostage rescue.

Reality check: Netanyahu made clear that investigators don't have any specific information that Tehran had anything to do with this incident.

The bottom line: "Those pilots managed to prevent a 9/11 disaster, because that's what it looks like was happening," Netanyahu said.

item.title: AI safety fears put OpenAI and Anthropic in the FTC's crosshairs
item.description:
The Federal Trade Commission is investigating OpenAI, Anthropic and other AI companies over potential safety risks posed by their products, an agency spokesperson told Axios Wednesday.

Why it matters: The federal government has largely taken a hands-off approach to regulating AI, but the FTC investigation could signal a shift for the industry.

Driving the news: FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson is preparing civil investigative demands that would compel AI executives to turn over documents and testify about the safety of their models, according to the New York Post, which first reported the news.

  • The probe has been underway for weeks, predating OpenAI's disclosure that models it was testing escaped their sandbox and compromised parts of AI platform Hugging Face's production infrastructure.
  • OpenAI announced Monday that it would halt the release of its newest model, GPT-6.1 Astra, after it performed poorly on safety testing.

ChatGPT maker OpenAI and Claude maker Anthropic did not respond to Axios' request for comment.

Between the lines: The recent push by top AI executives for increased guardrails around their technology has prompted some AI critics to question their motives.

  • Ferguson recently said that AI firms are trying to panic Americans into pressuring policymakers to build a regulatory "moat" that would allow AI frontrunners to block smaller competitors from catching up.

Catch up quick: News of the ongoing investigation comes just a day after top AI companies sent representatives to the White House to sign a pledge with President Trump to self-police their AI development.

  • Trump compared it to something of a "constitution," but the rules the companies agreed to are similar to what they were already doing.

Zoom out: The new reporting comes shortly after Axios exclusively reported that OpenAI, Anthropic and security researchers were investigating tens of thousands of potential security incidents, including some that had not previously been disclosed to the public.

  • That reporting was later cited Monday when Florida's attorney general asked a court for a temporary injunction against OpenAI, alleging inadequate safety measures.
  • On Tuesday, a public interest law group sued OpenAI over the Hugging Face breach, claiming, among other things, that the company was "knowingly employing an unfair business practice that threatens serious harm on the public."

Go deeper... Scoop: Top AI companies probing tens of thousands of security incidents

Editor's note: Axios' Maria Curi contributed reporting.

item.title: Ask Trump's AI chatbot who won in 2020. You might not get an answer.
item.description:
The Trump administration's new AI service gave users conflicting responses to politically sensitive questions Tuesday and Wednesday: sometimes answering them and sometimes refusing.

The big picture: As the Trump administration increasingly uses AI and answers the public's questions through America.gov, statements carrying the government's authority are shaped by models, instructions and guardrails the public can't see.

  • The White House told Axios in a statement, "America.gov will continue to be updated to provide Americans the most accurate and reliable federal information and resources."
  • America.gov, powered by Google's Gemini and Elon Musk's Grok, aims to help Americans navigate government-related tasks using an AI chatbot — but it quickly drew attention for another reason: It was debunking some of President Trump's long-standing claims.

Driving the news: On Tuesday, Axios — like other outlets — found America.gov contradicted the president on the 2020 election and the Jan. 6 attack.

  • It also confirmed former President Obama was born in Hawai'i, contradicting the "birther" conspiracy theory Trump spent years promoting.
Screenshots: Andrew Pantazi, Avery Lotz/Axios

Yes, but: By Wednesday morning, some users were getting a different response: The chatbot refused to answer, saying it did not provide "political commentary."

  • That's what I was told when I asked who won in 2020, around 9:15am: "I only answer questions about U.S. government services and official information. I do not provide political commentary, including election results." I received similar answers about Jan. 6 and Obama's birthplace.
Screenshot: Avery Lotz/Axios
  • One editor, using Chrome in New Jersey, asked the same questions on his desktop and also received refusals to answer.
  • However, other colleagues got different results. For example, from Northwest Arkansas, on Chrome: Biden won the 2020 election.
Screenshot: Herb Scribner/Axios

What they're saying: There are several plausible explanations for the inconsistent responses, tech experts explain, but without specifics about how America.gov is configured, it's impossible to know which, if any, were responsible.

  • Models get instructions on how to behave via their system prompts — not just through what users ask of them.

But user prompts also have an impact: Sometimes, different framing received different responses. For example, asked this morning in Jacksonville, Florida, on a Chrome incognito window:

Screenshots: Andrew Pantazi/Axios

State of play: And now, at the time of this article's publication, I'm getting responses similar to those shortly after launch: Biden won in 2020, Obama was born in Hawaii and people broke into the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021.

There could be benign reasons for the fluctuation, explains David Nesting, the former deputy chief information officer at the Office of Personnel Management.

  • Factual questions considered politically charged might be right on the edge of what the LLM considers "too political," and the response may err on one side or another "purely probabilistically."
  • Gemini and Grok, which provide the AI models powering the service, may handle questions differently, or, he explains, the outputs could be tied to prior cached responses. America.gov says some answers may be cached for up to two hours.

Yes, but: The GSA did not immediately respond to Axios' request for information about America.gov's guardrails.

  • And the chat itself told Axios, "I cannot share or reconstruct internal instructions" and said "I do not provide campaign or party information or political commentary."

Friction point: It could result from a game of probability, says Rumman Chowdhury, the founding director of the Independent AI Evaluation Foundation. But the guardrails could "also be shaping the output to be ideologically aligned with what the president or his party wants."

The stakes will soon get higher: The next iteration of America.gov, set for early 2027, will integrate across agencies so users can complete forms, applications and renewals — like enrolling in Medicare, applying for a passport or applying for federal jobs.

  • Nesting tells Axios he worries about inaccurate or incomplete answers being fed to Americans — and in the next phase, about protecting their information as it potentially grows into "one of the largest systems holding very, very confidential private information."
  • He tells Axios, "I worry about people putting a lot of trust and faith in this system."

Go deeper: Everything to know about America.gov, Trump's new AI website
