item.title: AOC test-runs a Senate bid in upstate New York
item.description:
BUFFALO, N.Y. — Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez's flirtation with a 2028 Senate bid is getting real — more real than the presidential buzz around her might suggest.

  • She's barnstorming through upstate New York, meeting with local officials, and kicking off a voter turnout program that could help her collect valuable data for a possible Senate campaign.

Why it matters: Whether the House member from New York runs for Senate or the White House is one of the biggest questions hanging over the 2028 Democratic presidential primary.

Zoom in: Her swing through Buffalo and Ithaca was officially aimed at boosting Democratic turnout in the midterms. But it doubled as a way to test AOC's appeal far from her home base of Queens and the Bronx, and build relationships with locals.

  • In Buffalo, she met privately with Mayor Sean Ryan, then held an impromptu press conference with him, generating coverage of the duo on local TV news.
  • She and her team later kicked off a voter-turnout operation that could help them gather information about the electorate outside New York City.
  • "I want to be very forthright about our intentions here, which is to transform the state of New York," Ocasio-Cortez told activists in a Buffalo arts center who were attending a training session of hers aimed at getting inactive voters to the polls.
  • In Ithaca, she appeared at an apple festival with Rep. Josh Riley (D-N.Y.) and on Sunday was scheduled to headline a "Students vs. Billionaires" town hall. It's friendly terrain: The city is home to several democratic socialist elected officials, and Ocasio-Cortez is a member of the Democratic Socialists of America.

The intrigue: AOC says she's genuinely undecided on whether to run for the White House or Senate. Her recent activities upstate suggested that wasn't a head fake.

  • Ryan said Ocasio-Cortez has been talking with state officials about how help communities beyond New York City.
  • Meanwhile, some influential Democrats in early presidential primary states have told us they haven't yet heard from AOC. And she hasn't made public visits this year to some of those early states, a contrast from other potential 2028 contenders who are practically living in them.

Many political insiders believe that if Ocasio-Cortez were to run for an open Senate seat, she'd clear the Democratic field.

  • Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), who's in his fifth term, hasn't said whether he'll run for reelection.
  • AOC was greeted like a rock star on her upstate tour, with Ryan remarking that at City Hall "a young man really, literally shouted across the lobby, like, 'Oh my gosh, congresswoman, can I take a picture with you?'"

Yes, but: Ocasio-Cortez also has taken several steps that could point toward a presidential run. She's toured the country, moderated her stance on some cultural issues, and opened up about her egg-freezing journey.

  • She recently told the New York Times she'll consider whether to run for president after the midterms.

Between the lines: One exchange with Ocasio-Cortez offered a window into how she is approaching her decision.

  • We asked her how she's thinking about the future of the progressive movement as she weighs a White House run. In the last two open Democratic presidential primaries, there has been a clear progressive standard-bearer, and many on the left think she's their only hope for 2028.
  • She didn't seem persuaded that by that argument.
  • "The movement is so much bigger than any one person," she told us.

The bottom line: AOC suggested that her choice won't be solely about ideology.

  • "These decisions aren't always about punditry or ideology. It's about putting the country first," she said. "What's important is ending … the corrupt reign of the Trump administration, as well as any of its acolytes."
  • Asked whether that means she's weighing "electability" as she determines her next move, she replied, "I don't see who wouldn't."

item.title: Amodei critics target Trump with hit piece before White House dinner
item.description:
Opponents of Anthropic's Dario Amodei are circulating a highly negative brief about him to the White House ahead of an important dinner with President Trump, per an Axios review of the document.

Why it matters: No company wants to be on Trump's bad side — and a Sunday night dinner between the president and Amodei could be what thaws relations after a year of tension.

Behind the scenes: The brief, which is not an internal White House document, casts Amodei as having "a long record of attacking Trump" and having "deep Democratic ties."

  • It notes the company's falling out earlier this year with the Pentagon as a "clear example of Dario showing he doesn't trust President Trump."
  • The brief is intended for Trump's eyes and is likely to get in front of him, according to a source familiar with the internal workings of the White House. Its origin is unclear.
  • It even reads in "Trump Talk," a name the president gives to his style of posting: "Dario claimed that AI would eliminate half of all entry-level white collar jobs as soon as this year. WRONG!"

Between the lines: The brief's creators are appealing to a president who prizes loyalty and puts a premium on praise.

  • Amodei's failure to communicate properly with the Trump administration has previously cost the company.
  • Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Yes, but: Trump has also been laser-focused on winning the AI race and Anthropic is one of the few companies on the frontier of the technology.

  • Anthropic is also valued at hundreds of billions of dollars and has plans to go public soon, making it even harder for the White House to ignore.
  • "The WH is trying to get everyone seated at the table," one source told Axios.

The bottom line: Anthropic and the White House both have something to gain from Sunday night's dinner, so long as Amodei's critics don't get there first.

Marc Caputo contributed to this story

item.title: Trump: 5 terrorism suspects in U.K. base incident were under investigation
item.description:
British police arrested five men Sunday on suspicion of terrorism near a U.K. air base used for U.S. operations in Iran, as President Trump said the suspects had been under investigation.

The latest: "Working with Britain, it was an amazing job," Trump told reporters Sunday morning. "We had them under investigation. They were looking to do big damage to our fort, and working with the British worked out great and we got them."

The big picture: Officials declared a major incident and set up roadblocks overnight near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, southwestern England.

  • The incident, which British investigators did not immediately link to Tehran, comes one day after Trump said he'd rejected the latest Iranian proposal to end the war — though he told Axios's Barak Ravid on Sunday that he expects fresh talks this week.

State of play: Police received a call around 12.45 a.m. Sunday local time relating to "three suspicious vehicles" that appeared to be traveling towards the air base used by the U.S. 501st Combat Support Wing and the 420th Air Base Squadron, per a Metropolitan Police statement.

  • Armed officers responded in the area of Whelford, a village some 33 miles from the city of Oxford. There they arrested the men "on suspicion of committing offenses under the Explosives Act" and they were further arrested "on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act, contrary to section 5 of the Terrorism Act," according to the statement.

Zoom in: U.K. counter-terrorism official Vicki Evans said officers established a 400-meter cordon (roughly a quarter-mile) around vehicles in the area while the British Army's Explosive Ordnance Disposal unit conducted examinations.

  • "As a precaution, around 85 households have been evacuated whilst these examinations take place," she said in a statement.
  • A nearby leisure centre was opened for people evacuated from the area.

Context: RAF Fairford is the U.S. Air Force's preferred bomber forward operating location in Europe and supports a variety of missions and exercises throughout the year, according to the Air Force.

Flashback: Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps warned in July that any base used for attacks on Iranian territory would be considered a "legitimate target" in a statement that specifically referenced U.S. B-1 bombers flying from RAF Fairford.

What they're saying: The 501st Combat Support Wing told Axios that no U.S. Air Force personnel were involved in the incident.

  • "The 501st Combat Support Wing appreciates the swift response and continued support of our local law enforcement partners," the statement said. "We remain in close coordination with our UK partners to help ensure the safety and security of both our military and local communities."

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details throughout.

item.title: Scoop: Anthropic's Dario Amodei to have White House dinner with Trump
item.description:
President Trump plans to host Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei at a private White House dinner on Sunday evening, sources familiar told Axios.

Why it matters: The dinner —the first one-on-one meeting between the two— is an indication of thawing relations between Anthropic and the administration, whose officials and allies have had longstanding tensions.

Driving the news: Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson plan to meet top AI CEOs Tuesday at the White House, and this friendly dinner serves as an appetizer.

  • Top tech CEOs from OpenAI's Sam Altman to Google's Sundar Pichai flanked Trump during a state dinner last week but there was one notable exception —Amodei, who had a scheduling conflict.
  • Afterward, Trump personally invited Amodei to the dinner, one of the sources said.

The big picture: Anthropic's relationship with the administration has been on shaky ground all year, with signs of warming quickly deteriorating thereafter.

Between the lines: Amodei is such a quirky and controversial figure in AI that he has started to enter mainstream pop culture.

  • Amodei was mocked on the latest episode of Saturday Night Live over his personality traits and his views on AI safety.
  • Last week, Trump allies circulated talking points to the White House that emphasized Amodei's role in, and the oddities of, the effective altruism movement.
  • Months ago, when Anthropic first started talking about having a one-on-one with Trump, some advised against it because "Dario's a little too weird" for Trump, one senior official told Axios.

What they are saying: "President Trump has been clear: America will lead the world in Super Intelligence, while protecting American consumers," a White House official said.

  • "We will drive innovation, strengthen American competitiveness, and ensure this transformative technology works for the American people."

The bottom line: In an administration that is so closely attuned to the president's moods and personal relationships, a sit down with Trump at the White House is priceless for any company.

item.title: After nixing Iran proposal, Trump tells Axios he expects talks this week
item.description:
One day after he rejected an Iranian proposal to end the war, President Trump told Axios in a phone interview on Sunday that he expects U.S. negotiators to engage in more talks with the country this week.

Why it matters: Qatar and other regional mediators are trying to revive negotiations between the U.S. and Iran, but the two sides are far apart on the key issues.

  • While Iran wants to focus any talks on the Strait of Hormuz and the U.S. naval blockade, the Trump administration is demanding that Iran agree to nuclear concessions.
  • Two regional sources confirmed Trump's comment about more talks this week. They said they expect another round of indirect dialogue between the U.S. and Iran as early as Monday. But it isn't clear if the gaps can be bridged.

What he's saying: "I expect more talks with Iran [this week]. They want to make a deal, but it is not the deal that I want to make. It is what we would have maybe agreed to a year ago. They overplayed their hand," Trump said.

  • Asked if he is considering resuming strikes against Iran, Trump said: "I am always thinking about it."

State of play: In the meantime, Trump said, the U.S. military is facilitating a lot of oil out of the Strait of Hormuz.

  • He said that over the weekend the largest amount of oil transited through the strait since the war began. "More than 20 million barrels," Trump said.
  • A U.S. defense official confirmed Trump's assertion, saying that on Friday night 22 million barrels of oil were exported through the strait.

Driving the news: U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held a new round of indirect negotiations with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York last Tuesday.

  • Qatari officials participated, passing messages between the two sides.
  • Araghchi delivered to Witkoff and Kushner Iran's conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz and resuming nuclear talks.
  • Iran proposed reopening the strait and restarting nuclear talks in a week, if the U.S. lifts its naval blockade, removes sanctions on oil sales and reinstates a ceasefire across the region.
  • Trump rejected the Iranian proposal on Saturday.

Behind the scenes: But a U.S. official and two regional sources told Axios that Qatari mediators are continuing shuttle diplomacy to try to reach a deal.

  • On Thursday, the prime minister of Qatar met in New York with the Iranian president and discussed the potential deal with the Trump administration.
  • Shortly after, senior Qatari officials met Witkoff and briefed him.
  • A regional source with knowledge of the indirect negotiations said the Qatari mediators discussed the original Iranian proposal with both parties and provided a compromise proposal to both sides to review.

What to watch: Over the weekend, the Qatari mediators have been going back and forth separately with Iranian and U.S. negotiators on changes to the text.

  • Qatari mediators are expected to meet separately with Araghchi and Witkoff as early as Monday.

The other side: Araghchi told NBC on Sunday that despite Trump's rejection of the Iranian proposal, Iran still wants a diplomatic solution.

  • He said that the midterm elections aren't part of Iran's calculations. "We only care about our national interests. We are ready for negotiations," he said.
  • "Although we heard from President Trump that he's rejecting this deal ... we are still waiting for an official response through the mediators," Araghchi added.
item.content:encoded:
One day after he rejected an Iranian proposal to end the war, President Trump told Axios in a phone interview on Sunday that he expects U.S. negotiators to engage in more talks with the country this week.

Why it matters: Qatar and other regional mediators are trying to revive negotiations between the U.S. and Iran, but the two sides are far apart on the key issues.

  • While Iran wants to focus any talks on the Strait of Hormuz and the U.S. naval blockade, the Trump administration is demanding that Iran agree to nuclear concessions.
  • Two regional sources confirmed Trump's comment about more talks this week. They said they expect another round of indirect dialogue between the U.S. and Iran as early as Monday. But it isn't clear if the gaps can be bridged.

What he's saying: "I expect more talks with Iran [this week]. They want to make a deal, but it is not the deal that I want to make. It is what we would have maybe agreed to a year ago. They overplayed their hand," Trump said.

  • Asked if he is considering resuming strikes against Iran, Trump said: "I am always thinking about it."

item.title: The most pressing midterm issues for rural voters
item.description:
Data: KFF/AP Rural Voters Survey; Chart: Herb Scribner

Cost of living and health care costs top the list of issues rural voters want 2026 midterm candidates to address, according to a new AP/KFF poll.

The big picture: Ahead of the midterms, rural voters rank pocketbook concerns above immigration, the conflict with Iran and several major domestic policy debates.

By the numbers: 69% of rural voters said it is 'extremely important' for candidates to talk about the cost of living, followed by health care costs (56%) and fraud in government programs (54%).

Context: The AP/KFF poll asked 2,241 registered voters living in rural areas how important it was for 2026 candidates to talk about each of eight issues.

Cost of living concerns

Zoom in: Affordability concerns extend across a wide range of everyday expenses.

  • 57% of rural voters cited an economic concern — including rising costs, jobs, wages and housing affordability — when asked about the biggest issue facing their local community.
  • 67% said they were at least somewhat worried about affording gas or transportation, while 66% said the same about health care and 60% about food and groceries.
  • Three-quarters rated the cost of living in their area as either "fair" or "poor," up 25 percentage points from 2017.
Data: KFF/AP Rural Voters Survey; Chart: Herb Scribner

Reality check: Rural voters' unhappiness with costs doesn't necessarily translate into support for Democrats.

  • According to the poll, 40% trust Republicans more to handle the cost of living, compared with 25% who trust Democrats and 27% who trust neither party.
  • Rural voters in the survey leaned Republican: 54% identified as GOP voters or Republican-leaning independents, while 32% identified as Democrats or Democratic-leaning independents.

What we're watching: Whether economic frustration affects voter enthusiasm among rural Republicans.

  • 27% of rural Republican voters disapprove of Trump's handling of the economy, per the poll. Among them, 59% say they're absolutely certain to vote in the midterms.
  • Still, 98% of rural Republicans say they're more likely to vote for a Republican than a Democrat.

The fine print: The KFF/AP poll surveyed 2,241 registered voters living in rural areas nationwide from Aug. 12-24, 2026, online and by phone. The margin of sampling error is ±3 percentage points.

item.title: It's a 5% world. We're just living in it
item.description:
The cost of borrowing money is moving unrelentingly higher, with profound implications for savers, borrowers and the U.S. government's fiscal outlook.

The big picture: The bond market moves over the last few weeks have pushed most risk-free interest rates north of 5%.

  • Barring a rapid reversal, expect pain to come in interest-sensitive sectors like housing, new stress on federal government finances and greater risks of financial disruption.
  • It is better news for savers, who have taken paper losses on existing bonds in recent weeks but can now deploy cash safely with the best prospective returns seen in decades.

Zoom out: It is clearer than ever that the era of cheap borrowing and abundant capital that lasted from 2008 to 2021 is well and truly over.

  • Every individual looking to take a home mortgage or car loan is in competition with the voracious capital needs of the AI giants and the U.S. government.
  • While the Federal Reserve has gotten out of the business of forecasting its next moves, it is now looking out of position. Its leaders increasingly believe that it has set its policy rates too low to control inflation amid a growth boom, and are now looking to adjust course, which means last week's rate hike won't be the last.
  • Rate hikes may not deter much AI investment or government borrowing, which leaves all other interest-sensitive sectors to bear the brunt of bringing the economy into better balance.

Zoom in: The surge in rates has been driven for the most part by a rise in real yields — implying a stronger growth outlook, not an outburst in expected inflation.

  • Investors can now buy a 30-year inflation-protected Treasury security that pays 3.26%, the highest since 2002. This time five years ago, that number was negative.
  • The forward earnings yield of the S&P 500 is about 5%. With the 30-year nominal Treasury bond yielding around 5.5%, bonds look more attractive relative to stocks than they have in ages.

State of play: The recent surge in longer-term rates is poised to push 30-year fixed-rate mortgages to near 8%. Mortgage News Daily on Thursday clocked the 30-year rate at 7.45%, or 7.55% for jumbo loans.

  • Mortgage rates got that high briefly in the fall of 2023, but the last time they were above that level on a sustained basis was in 2000.
  • Over time, the housing market can find a balance. But in the near term, surges in rates just mean pain as the market freezes up.
  • People can't afford to buy houses with 7.5%+ rates, and sellers don't want to cut their prices, so there is a standstill, as witnessed in the fall of 2023, until either rates fall or prices adjust.

The intrigue: Higher rates, if sustained, will make America's fiscal situation considerably thornier.

  • The U.S. government's debt service costs were already projected to reach new highs in the coming years — but that burden will be much worse if the rate surge of the last few weeks is sustained.

By the numbers: In projections that the Congressional Budget Office produced last February, net interest costs are already at $1 trillion this year and on track to reach $2 trillion by 2035, meaning that much of federal spending is needed just to service old bills.

  • But those projections assumed 10-year Treasury yields were in the ballpark of 4.3%. They're now nearly a full percentage point higher than that.
  • In startling numbers that CBO released this week, in a scenario in which interest rates were 1 percentage point higher than its baseline, debt held by the public would grow to 222% of GDP in 2056, 47 percentage points higher than the baseline.

Reality check: Higher interest rates don't flow through to government debt service costs immediately. Longer-term bonds gradually mature over time.

  • So a reversal in rates would help the fiscal arithmetic (at least so long as it wasn't caused by a recession or productivity slump).

The bottom line: If the 5% world is here to stay, it commands a rethinking of the U.S. government's tax and spending policies, the price of assets, and more generally what we consider normal in an era of steep global demand for capital.

  • And that adjustment is in its early days.

item.title: Scoop: "Delusional" Senate forecast rattles Sea Island retreat
item.description:
A pollster for Senate Republicans was met with disbelief on Saturday after telling GOP donors and operatives that they could grow their majority in November's midterm elections, sources tell Axios.

Why it matters: "Delusional," one attendee at the National Republican Senatorial Committee's Sea Island retreat in Georgia told Axios after the presentation by the pollster, Erik Iverson. "The mood is not good," said another.

  • "I think most attendees down here are politically astute and realistic about the headwinds Republicans face," said a third.
  • A fourth attendee described conversations at the event as Republicans sarcastically telling each other "we're winning" and "everything's good."
  • The Sea Island fall retreat is a major donor event for the NRSC each cycle, attracting big-dollar donors, senators and their senior staff.

The details: Iverson, a former Montana Republican Party chair, suggested that Republicans could net gain one seat in the Senate after the midterms, but did not provide a state-by-state explanation for how they would do so, sources said.

  • Another source in the room said Iverson's comments were in the context of a question about the 2022 midterms, when Senate Democrats picked up a seat despite former President Biden's poor polling numbers.
  • Some in the room laughed when a member of the audience asked if it meant Republicans would also pick up a seat, the source said.

What he's saying: "I told attendees that I think all incumbent Republican Senators will hold their seats because we have good candidates who are well funded," Iverson told Axios.

  • "And I pointed out that in 2022 President Biden's image was double digits under water in every single swing Senate seat yet Democrats still gained a seat.  The message was for folks to keep their heads up," he added.
  • Iverson presented polling findings on gas prices and data centers at a separate event earlier last week, according to slides obtained by Axios.
  • It included that 60% of swing voters would consider supporting new data centers in their state if they met community requirements such as paying all their energy costs and not negatively affecting local water supplies.

Between the lines: Attendees questioned why they were not given a full update on each race.

  • The surprisingly competitive Texas race was not discussed at all, some sources noted.

Zoom in: Other speakers on Saturday included NRSC Chair Tim Scott (R-S.C.), Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W. Va.), Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) and NRSC political director Brendan Jaspers.

  • There was also a panel with Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) and Senate candidates Julia Letlow (Louisiana), Kevin Hern (Oklahoma), Andy Barr (Kentucky) and Harriet Hageman (Wyoming).

The big picture: Top Senate Republicans openly acknowledge they face a tough map in November.

  • Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) told Axios on Wednesday that it's a "tough environment."
  • The NRSC itself is asking donors for $9 million to help in three states — Alaska, Iowa and Ohio — where President Trump won by double digits in 2024, as Axios scooped on Thursday.

Editor's note: This story has been corrected to note that Iverson presented polling findings on gas prices and data centers at a separate event earlier last week (not at the Sea Island event on Saturday).
